by that may Indra, Varuṇa, and Bṛhaspati, the guardians of the world, cause us to swell.
Sing forth a beautiful hymn for the prize-winning contest of cattle; bestow auspicious riches upon us!
Lead this sacrifice of ours to the gods; may the streams of clarified butter flow pure and honey-sweet. 1.
In me I take Agni first, together with dominion, splendor, and strength.
In me I place progeny, in me I place long life—*svāhā*! In me [I place] Agni. 2.
Right here, O Agni, maintain wealth for us; let not those who were previously hostile bring you low.
Through your sovereign power, O Agni, may [the world] be well-governed for you; may your worshipper increase, unsubdued.
Agni has looked along the forefront of the dawns; Jātavedas, as the first, has looked along the days.
He has entered along the sun, along the dawns, along the rays, and along heaven and earth. 4.
Agni has looked out toward the forefront of the dawns; as the first Jātavedas, he has looked out toward the days.
He has looked out toward the many rays of the sun; he has stretched himself across heaven and earth. 5.
Clarified butter is yours, O Agni, in the divine dwelling; with clarified butter Manu kindles you today.
May the divine daughters bring clarified butter for you; may the cows yield clarified butter for you, O Agni.
O King Varuṇa, your golden house is built within the waters;
from there, may the King, firm in his vows, release us from all bonds.
O King Varuṇa, from every bond, from every bond, release us here.
Whatever we have said, "O Waters, O Invincible One," or "O Varuṇa," from that, O Varuṇa, release us. //2//
O Varuṇa, loosen the uppermost bond from us, untie the lowest, and release the middle one.
Then, O Āditya, being blameless before you, may we abide in your law for the sake of Aditi.
O Varuṇa, release from us all those snares—those which are highest or lowest, those that belong to Varuṇa.
Drive away from us bad dreams and misfortune; then may we go to the world of the righteous. 4.
Invincible, Jātavedas, immortal, sovereign, O Agni, bearer of dominion, shine here;
releasing all maladies, protect our household today with your auspicious human-like [powers]. //1//
O Indra, you were born for the sake of desirable dominion and power, O bull among the peoples.
You drove away the unfriendly folk and made wide space for the gods. //2//
Like a fearsome wild beast, roaming and dwelling in the mountains, may he come hither from the farthest distance.
Having sharpened your bolt and whetted your keen edge, O Indra, strike down the enemies and drive away the adversaries.
That very one, the prize-winning steed, impelled by the gods, the victorious, the overcomer of chariots;
the swift Tārkṣya with uninjured fellies, the winner in battle—we invoke him here for our well-being. 1.

I call upon Indra the protector, Indra the helper, the hero Indra who is easily invoked at every invocation; I now call upon the mighty Indra, invoked by many. May the bounteous Indra grant us well-being. //1//
Rudra who is in the fire, who is within the waters, who has entered the herbs and the plants—he who fashioned all these worlds: let there be homage to that Rudra, to Agni. //1//
Go away! You are an enemy, or you are indeed an enemy. You have mixed poison with poison, or you have indeed mixed poison itself. Go toward the serpent alone; slay him! //1//
I have drawn near to the celestial waters; we have been united with their essence.
Rich in milk, O Agni, I have come; endow me with splendor. //1//
O Agni, unite me with splendor, unite me with progeny, and unite me with long life.
May the gods take note of this of mine; may Indra, together with the seers, take note.
O Waters, carry away this: whatever is blameworthy and whatever is impurity;
whatever treachery and falsehood, and whatever curse I have uttered against the innocent.
You are fuel; may I prosper. You are kindling; may I prosper together with you. You are splendor; bestow splendor upon me. 4.
Tear it away as of old, like the coiled-up tangle of a creeper;
strike down the power of the Dāsa.
(7.90.2a) May we divide among ourselves that accumulated wealth of his with Indra’s aid.
(7.90.2c) By the decree of Varuṇa, I cause your bright flame to fade away. 2.
So that the penis may fall away and remain unproductive among women—
of Avastha, of Knadīvat, of Śāṅkura, the piercer—
whatever is extended, let that be unextended; whatever is contracted, let that be contracted.
May Indra, the good protector, the possessor of wealth, through his aids, be gracious to us—he who possesses all knowledge.
May he drive away our enemies and grant us fearlessness; may we be masters of heroic vigor. //1//
May that Indra, the good protector and possessor of wealth, drive our enemies far away from us.
May we abide in the favor of that worshipful one, and likewise in his auspicious goodwill. 1.
With Indra and with fury, may we overcome those who attack us, slaying the obstructors without resistance. //1//
With the firm oblation, we lead Soma forward with firmness, so that Indra may make our subjects entirely his own and of one mind. //1//
Upward have his two dark, trembling, greedy ones flown like birds to heaven;
they are the two burners of his heart, the scorcher and the inflamer.
I have raised these two up, like two oxen exhausted from labor,
like two barking dogs, or like two springing wolves.
The piercers, the thrusters, and those that pierce all around— I bind the penis of that man or woman who has brought [this] from here. //3//
The cows have settled in their place; the bird has flown to its dwelling.
The mountains stand firm in their station; I have fixed the two kidneys in their place.
Since we have chosen you here today, O wise Hotṛ, as this sacrifice proceeds—O most powerful one, firm and steadfast, come to the Soma, knowing well the sacrifice. //1//

O Indra, Lord of the Bay Horses, unite us with a favorable mind, with cattle, with wise patrons, and with well-being; unite us with the sacred prayer established by the gods, and with the benevolent favor of the worshipful deities.
O divine Agni, send back to their own dwelling those willing gods whom you brought hither;
having eaten and drunk the sweet draughts, O Vasus, bestow riches upon this man. //3//
O gods, we have prepared easy paths for you who have come to this libation with pleasure;
carrying and bringing your own treasures, ascend to heaven after the wealthy *gharma*.
O sacrifice, go to the sacrifice; go to the lord of the sacrifice.
Go to your own womb; svāhā!
This is your sacrifice, O Lord of Sacrifice, accompanied by the hymn of praise;
may it be rich in heroic power—*svāhā*!
Vaṣaṭ to those who have sacrificed, vaṣaṭ to those who have not sacrificed!
O gods who know the way, having found the way, go upon the way! 7.7.7
O Lord of the mind, carry this sacrifice of ours to the gods in heaven.
Svāhā! To heaven! Svāhā! To earth! Svāhā! To the intermediate space! Svāhā! I place it in the wind. Svāhā! //8//

The sacrificial grass is anointed with the oblation of clarified butter; together with Indra, the Vasu, and the Maruts, together with the gods, the Viśvedevas—let the oblation, thus anointed, go to Indra. Svāhā!
Strew around; enclose the altar. Do not steal the kinswoman lying there.
This golden, green seat for the Hotṛ-priest—these are the neck-ornaments in the world of the sacrificer.
I turn away from the evil dream, from the bad dream, and from misfortune. I place the sacred word (*brahman*) between us; let the sorrows that have dreams as their mouth be driven far away.
Whatever food I eat in a dream that is not found in the morning—may all that be auspicious for me, for it is not seen by day. //1//
Having paid homage to Heaven and Earth, to the Intermediate Space, and to Death, I stir [the fire] while standing upright; may the powerful lords not harm me. //1//
Which Kṣatriya, seeking welfare, will lead us out from this blameless deceit?
Who, desiring sacrifice, or who desiring fulfillment, seeks long life among the gods? //1//
Who, delighting in friendship with Bṛhaspati, shall fashion his bodies at will—[he who receives] the speckled cow, well-milking and always with her calf, given by Varuṇa to Atharvan? //1//
Departing from what belongs to men and choosing the divine word, turn back toward our guidance together with all your friends.

Whatever we have done through lack of mindfulness, O Agni, or whatever we have failed in our conduct, O Jātavedas—protect us from that, O wise one; for our welfare, let there be immortality for us, your friends. //1//
From heaven down, the seven rays of the sun bring them across;
the waters of the ocean, those flowing streams, have caused the barb to fall away. 1.

Whether it be one who seeks to harm us by stealth or one who seeks to harm us openly, O Agni, whether he be a stranger or one of our own kin—let him go back, toothless and powerless. Let neither his dwelling nor his offspring remain for us, O Agni.
O Jātavedas, whoever should seek to harm us— whether we are sleeping or waking, standing still or moving— do thou,
in harmony with Vaiśvānara as thy companion, burn them down, O Jātavedas, turning toward them.
This homage to the fierce, tawny one who has mastery over his own body through the dice:
with clarified butter I propitiate Kali; may he be gracious to us in such a state.
O Agni, carry ghee for the Apsarases; carry dust for the dice, sand, and water.
Rejoicing in the offering of the oblation according to their respective portions, may the gods delight in both kinds of offerings.
The Apsarases rejoice in the communal feast between the sun and the oblation-holder.
May they anoint my hands with clarified butter; may they deliver my rival, the gambler, into my power. //3//
Reveal the danger to the one who plays against us; drench us with clarified butter!
Strike down like a tree with a lightning bolt him who plays against us. //4//

He who has made this wealth for our gaming, he who [determined] the casting of the dice and the remainder—may that god, enjoying this oblation, rejoice with the Gandharvas in our shared revelry. //5//
"O you who dwell together," such is your name; for you, the dice, are fierce-looking upholders of the kingdom.
To you, O Indus, we shall pay worship with an oblation; may we be masters of riches.
Since I call upon the gods in my need, since we have lived the life of sacred study (brahmacarya),
and since I seize the brown dice— may they be gracious to us in such a state.
O Agni and Indra, for the donor, you two have slain the Vṛtras without resistance;
for you both are the greatest slayers of Vṛtra.

Those two by whom they first conquered the light of heaven, who have taken their stand over all the worlds—those two bulls of the people, with thunderbolts in their arms, Agni and Indra, the slayers of Vṛtra, I invoke. //2//
The god Bṛhaspati has approached you with the cup;
O Indra, enter among us with songs for the sake of the sacrificer who presses the soma. //3//
You are the belly of Indra, the container of Soma, the self of both gods and men.
Produce here offspring for us—those who are yours among these women, and those who are elsewhere; let them find delight here with you. //1//
Adorning heaven and earth, who are near with their benevolence and possess great ordinances—the seven divine waters have flowed forth; may they release us from distress.
May they release me from the curse of the oath, and also from that of Varuṇa; and also from the fetter of Yama, and from every offense against the gods.
O three-pronged one, O three-pronged weapon, cut down that [enemy], O three-pronged one,
so that those who hate the one who has performed [this rite] shall be deprived of their virility for him.
You are the pungent one, the pungent plant; you are poison, the destroyer of poison.
Like a discarded cow following after a bull, so are you cast aside.
I take from your flanks; I take from your heart.
From the very appearance of your mouth, I take all your splendor.
Let diseases depart, let anxieties depart, and let curses depart!
Let Agni slay the demonesses; let Soma slay those who seek to do harm.
Fly away from here, O evil Fortune; perish from here, fly away!
With an iron hook, we fasten you to our enemy. 1.
The ill-fated, unloved mark that has leaped upon me, like a creeper upon a tree—O Savitṛ, golden-handed, bestowing wealth upon us, place that elsewhere than here! 2.
A hundred and one fortunes have arisen together with the body from the birth of a mortal.
Of these, we cast out the most evil ones from here; O Jātavedas, bestow the auspicious ones upon us. 3.
I have distinguished these from those, like cows standing in a wasteland;
may the auspicious marks remain, and I have destroyed those that are evil.
Homage to Rūra, the shaker, the impeller, the bold one;
homage to Śīta, who fulfills former desires. //1//
He who comes upon this frog on one day or on two days— let that lawless one come upon him.
Come, O Indra, with your delightful bay horses whose hair is like peacock feathers;
let no one hold you back, as fowlers do not detain a bird—pass them by like a desert.
I cover your vital organs with armor; may King Soma clothe you with immortality.
May Varuṇa make for you a space wider than the wide; may the gods rejoice after you as you conquer. //1//
Homage to Antaka, to Death! May your out-breaths and in-breaths rest here.
May this man remain here together with his vital breaths, in the portion of the Sun, in the world of immortality. //1//
Bhaga has lifted him up; Soma, rich in stalks, has lifted him up.
The Maruts, the gods, have lifted him up, as have Indra and Agni for his well-being.
(8.1.3a) Here is your breath, O Asura; here is your life, here is your mind. (8.1.3c) We lift you up from the snares of Destruction with a divine word.
Step forth from here, O man; do not fall back! Casting off the fetter of death, do not be severed from this world, from the sight of Agni and Sūrya. //4//
For you let Vāta Mātariśvan blow; for you let the immortal waters rain down.
Let the sun shine pleasantly upon your body; may Death have pity on you—do not perish. //5//
(8.1.6a) This garden is not for you to descend upon, O man; I grant you life and skillful strength.
(8.1.6c) For mount this immortal, blissful chariot, and then, as one free from decay, you shall proclaim the assembly.
Let not your mind go there, nor let it vanish; do not abandon the living, nor follow the fathers.
May all the gods protect you here. (AVŚ 8.1.7)
Do not set your minds on those who have departed, who lead one away to the far distance;
ascend from darkness to the light, come hither, we take hold of your hands.
The dark one and the brindled one, the two dogs sent by Yama who guard the path—come hither;
do not hesitate, do not stand there with your mind turned away.
Do not follow this path; it is terrible. I tell you: do not go where you have not gone before.
O man, do not fall into that darkness. There is danger ahead, but safety behind you. {1} May the fires that dwell within the waters protect you; may the fire that men kindle protect you.
May Vaiśvānara Jātavedas protect you; let not the celestial lightning strike you down. 11.
Let not the flesh-eater harm you; move away from the ruinous pit. May Heaven protect you;
may Earth protect you. May the Sun and the Moon protect you; may the mid-air protect you from the missiles of the gods.
May awakening and watchfulness protect you; may sleeplessness and vigilance protect you; may the guardian and the watcher protect you. 13.
May they protect you; may they guard you. To them, homage! To them, svāhā! //14//
May Vāyu, Indra, Dhātṛ, and the protecting Savitṛ place you among the living beings in the ocean.
May breath and strength not forsake you; we summon your life-force back to you. 15.
Let not the jaw-joint nor darkness find you; let not the tongue perish upon the sacrificial grass. How might you be?
May the Ādityas and the Vasus lift you up, and may Indra and Agni [do so] for our well-being.
The sky has lifted you up, the earth has lifted you up, and Prajāpati has grasped you up.
From death, the plants whose king is Soma have carried you across.
O gods, let this man remain right here; let him not go from here to the other world.
By means of a thousandfold power, we cause him to cross over death.
I have carried you across from death; may those who bestow vital strength kindle you.
Let not women with disheveled hair, nor those weeping with harsh cries, bewail you.
I have brought you back; I have found you. You have returned, renewed. O whole-limbed one, I have found for you your entire sight and your entire lifespan.
Light has arisen for you; darkness has departed from you.
We cast away death, destruction, and consumption from you. Take hold of this attainment of immortality; may your life-span remain unbroken until old age.
I bring back to you this breath, this life; do not go to the dust or to the darkness; do not perish. //1//
Come hither toward the light of the living; I bring you back for a hundred autumns.
Releasing the snares of death and all ill-fortune, I bestow upon you a longer, further span of life.
From the wind I have found your breath; from the sun, I [have found] your eye.
That mind of yours which is within you, I maintain for you. Be conscious with your limbs; speak with your tongue, O speaker. 3.
With breath, I blow upon you, as one would kindle the fire at birth, among bipeds and quadrupeds.
Homage to your eye, O Death; homage to your breath have I paid. //4//
(5a) May this one live; let him not die! We cause him to rise up again. (5c) I prepare a remedy for him; O Death, do not slay the man! //5//
The life-giving, non-harming, living herb— protecting, conquering, and powerful— I invoke her here for his safety.
Speak for me; do not seize him! Let him remain here, belonging to you alone, with all his life intact.
O Bhava and Śarva, be gracious, grant us protection, ward off misfortune, and bestow long life upon us.

O Death, speak on his behalf; have mercy on him. Let him go from here unharmed, with all his limbs intact, hearing well, and reaching old age at a hundred years, may he enjoy prosperity through his own self. //8//
May the weapon of the gods avoid you; I carry you across, I have delivered you from the region of death.
Far away I drive off the flesh-eating fire; I set up a boundary for you so that you may live.
That path of yours, O Death, which leads through the dust and is unassailable—from that path we protect this man; as Brahmans, we make for him a protective armor.
I bestow upon you out-breath and in-breath, old age, death, long life, and well-being.
I ward off all those messengers of Yama sent by Vaivasvata as they roam about. 11.
Far away we drive off hostility, destruction, the seizer, the flesh-eaters, and the *piśācas*;
whatever *rakṣas* there is and every ill-being, that we strike away as if it were darkness. 12.
O Agni, from the immortal life of Jātavedas, I seek for you the breath of one who possesses long life.
So that you may not perish, being immortal and in harmony with all, I perform this for you; may it be fully accomplished for you. //13//
May Heaven and Earth be auspicious for you, free from heat, and full of splendor. May the sun shine warmly upon you; may the wind blow gently for your heart's sake.
May the celestial waters, rich with milk, flow auspiciously over you.
May the plants be auspicious for you; I have lifted you up from the lower earth toward the higher earth.
There, may both Ādityas, Sūrya and Candramas, protect you. 15.
Whatever garment is your upper robe, whatever girdle you fasten for yourself—may we make that auspicious for your body; may it be soft to the touch for you. 16.
When you, O barber, with a sharp-edged razor of great luster, shave the hair and beard, may you make our face beautiful; do not steal away our life-span. //17//
May rice and barley be auspicious for you—free from disease and free from hunger; these two drive away consumption and release one from distress.
Whatever you eat, whatever you drink—the milk of the cultivated grain, whatever is edible and whatever is inedible—I make all that food for you free from poison. 19.
To both day and night we entrust you;
from the *arāyas* that desire to devour, protect this one of mine.
We grant you a hundred, ten thousand, two, three, and four ages.
May Indra and Agni, and all the gods, grant their approval, being free from resentment. 21.
We entrust you to autumn, to winter, to spring, and to summer;
may the rains be pleasant for you, in which the plants flourish.
Death rules over bipeds; Death rules over quadrupeds.
Therefore, I lift you up from Death, the Lord of Cattle. Do not be afraid.
O unharmed one, you shall not die; you shall not die—do not fear!
Indeed, they do not die there, nor do they go to the lowest darkness. 24.
Everyone indeed lives there—the cow, the horse, the man, and the beast—where this sacred prayer (*brahman*) is performed as a protective enclosure for the sake of life. 25.
May he protect you from those of equal kin and from the sorcery of your own relatives.
Be unharmed, be immortal, live beyond [death]; let not your vital breaths abandon your body.
The hundred and one deaths, and the destructive powers that must be overcome—may the gods release you from them, from Agni Vaiśvānara. 27.

(8.2.28a) You are the body of Agni, the one who carries us across; you are the slayer of Rākṣasas, the slayer of rivals. (8.2.28c) Furthermore, you are the dispeller of disease; the Pūtudru tree is indeed a medicine.
{5} (8.3.1a) I anoint the Rākṣasa-slayer, the vigorous one; I approach for protection the most extensive friend.
Sharpening himself with our sacred rites, Agni has been kindled; may he protect us from harm by day and by night. //1//
O Jātavedas, kindled with your flame, touch the sorcerers with your iron fangs!
Seize the fools who worship false gods with your tongue; having devoured them, place the flesh-eaters in your mouth. 2.
Place both your jaws together, O you who know both; being a destroyer, sharpen the lower and the upper.
And, O Agni, roam through the mid-air and seize the sorcerers with your jaws.
O Agni, split open the skin of the sorcerer; let the destructive thunderbolt strike him down with its heat.
O Jātavedas, crush his joints asunder; let the flesh-eating, flesh-craving fire tear him apart.
O Agni Jātavedas, wherever you now see a sorcerer standing or moving about, or even flying in the intermediate space— pierce him with your arrow, whetting it as you shoot.
Bending your arrows with sacrifices, O Agni, and sharpening their points with your flames like thunderbolts—with those, pierce the sorcerers in the heart; break their arms back against them.
And, O Jātavedas, strike down those who have already set out, and the Yātudhānas with the spears of those who are setting out.
O Agni, blazing forth, strike them down first; let the ravenous vultures, the spotted ones, devour them raw.
Speak here, O Agni, which one is that sorcerer who does this?
Seize him with your fuel, O youngest one; deliver him over to the eye of the one who beholds men. //8//
With your sharp eye, O Agni, protect the sacrifice; lead it forward toward the Vasus, O wise one.
Let not the sorcerers deceive you as you blaze against the murderous demons, O watcher of men.
O watcher of men, look out for the *rakṣas* among the people; crush its three points.
O Agni, burn through its ribs with your heat; tear up the root of the sorcerer in three ways.
Let the sorcerer go three times into your snare, O Agni, he who strikes the Truth with falsehood.
O Jātavedas, flashing with your flame, bind him down right before the eyes of the one who praises you. //11//

O Agni, whatever curse a pair utters today, or whatever harshness of speech the chanters produce, and whatever arrow is born from the wrath of the mind—with that, pierce the sorcerers in their hearts. 12.
Crush the sorcerers with your heat; O Agni, crush the *rakṣas* with your flame.
Crush the fools who worship false gods with your radiance; crush those who thrive on life-breath as they burn away. 13.
May the gods today hear out the crookedness; may the released curses turn back against him.
May arrows strike the one who steals by speech in his vital parts; may the sorcerer fall into the snare of everyone. 14.
The sorcerer who anoints himself with human flesh, or with the flesh of a horse, or who steals the milk of the cow—O Agni, shatter their heads with your fiery heat! 15.
Let the sorcerers bring poison upon the cattle; let the evil-doers be cut down for Aditi.
May the god Savitṛ deliver them away; may they lose their share of the plants. 16.
The milk of the cow that belongs to the year—let not the sorcerer, O watcher of men, consume it!
O Agni, whichever one should desire to satisfy himself with the first-milked cream, pierce him in his vital organ with your flame as he turns toward you.
From of old, O Agni, you have crushed the sorcerers; the *rakṣas* have never conquered you in battles.
Burn up the flesh-eaters together with their roots; let none escape from your divine missile.
O Agni, protect us from below and from above; protect us from behind and from the front.
May those ageless and most burning flames of yours consume the one who utters evil against us. 19.
From behind, from before, from below, and from above, O Agni, as a seer protect us with your seer-power.
As an ageless friend for the sake of our aging, O Agni, you who are immortal, protect us mortals.
O Agni, bestow upon the singer that eye wherewith you behold the hoof-smiting sorcerers.
Like Atharvan, with divine light, burn away the unwise one who injures the truth. 21.
O Agni, O powerful one, we place you around us as a fortress— you, the inspired sage,
whose color is bold, the slayer of the treacherous day by day.
With poison, O Agni, strike down the treacherous Rākṣasas with your sharp flame and with your cresting, glowing rays.
Agni shines forth with great light; by his majesty, he makes all things manifest.
He overcomes the godless, malevolent illusions; he sharpens his two horns to gore the Rākṣasas.
O Jātavedas, those two horns of yours which are ageless, sharp-pointed, and sharpened by prayer—
with them, O Jātavedas, pierce with your flame the Kimīdin who assails us with an evil heart, turning him back toward you. 25.
Agni, the immortal with bright radiance, drives away the *rakṣas*—he who is pure, purifying, and worthy of praise.
O Indra and Soma, burn up the *rakṣas*; crush them and cast down those who increase in darkness, O Bulls.
Crush those who lack devotion; burn them down, strike them, and drive them away; sharpen your weapons against the devourers. //1//
O Indra and Soma, let the evil heat of the one who utters evil against us rise up like a cauldron placed upon the fire.
Against the hater of sacred prayer, the flesh-eater with the terrible eye, the *kimīdin*, bestow unremitting hatred.
O Indra and Soma, pierce the evildoers into the pit, into the darkness where there is no support, so that not even one of them may ever rise again; let that be your wrathful and conquering power.

O Indra and Soma, hurl down from heaven and from earth your weapon, the crusher of the one who speaks evil. Carve forth a thunderbolt from the mountains, with which you burn up the demon as it grows in strength.
O Indra and Soma, turn them back from heaven with your stone-hurling bolts, heated by fire!
With your unaging, heat-smiting weapons, pierce the devourers into the abyss; let them go forth voiceless.

O Indra and Soma, may this prayer encompass you from every side, as a girth encompasses two spirited horses. O lords of men, quicken with wisdom this sacrifice which I offer to you, and these sacred hymns.
Remember us with your impetuous deeds; strike down the treacherous, crooked-minded demons and Rākṣasas.
O Indra and Soma, let there be no easy path for the evil-doer who at any time seeks to harm me with malice. //7//
He who, with evil intent, accuses me with false words while I walk with a pure mind—may he, O Indra, be like water caught in the hollow of one’s hand; may the speaker of untruth come to naught.
Those who, by their ways, scatter the one who speaks simply, or those who corrupt what is auspicious with their own self-willed acts—
may Soma deliver them over to the serpent, or place them within the lap of Destruction.

O Agni, whoever seeks to harm our essence—whether that of our food, our horses, our cattle, or our bodies—let that enemy, thief, and doer of theft go to destruction; let him be deprived of both his body and his progeny.
Let him be far away from us in body and progeny; let him fall below all the three earths.
May the glory of him wither away, O gods, who seeks to harm me by day and by night. (11)
(8.4.12a) For the person who understands, the true and the untrue are easily distinguished; two words contend with one another.
(8.4.12c) Of these two, that which is the truth, whichever is more upright—that indeed Soma protects; he strikes down the untrue. //12//
Soma does not indeed further the crooked man, nor the Kṣatriya who holds [his office] falsely.
He slays the Rākṣasa; he slays the one who speaks with malice. Both lie within the snare of Indra. 13.
Whether I am one whose gods are false, or whether I have falsely invoked the gods, O Agni—why, O Jātavedas, are you angry with us? May those of deceitful speech fall into destruction! 14.14
May I die this very day if I am a sorcerer, or if I have burned a man with magic;
then may he be deprived of his ten sons who falsely calls me a sorcerer.
Whoever says of me, "O sorcerer," or whoever, being a *rakṣas*, says, "I am a sorcerer"—may Indra slay him with a great weapon; may he fall as the lowest of all living beings. (AVŚ 8.4.16)
She who comes forth at night like an owl, hiding her body from the malicious one—may she fall into the endless pit; may the pressing-stones strike down the demons with their clattering sounds.

Spread out, O Maruts, among the people; seek them out, seize the Rākṣasas, and grind them to pieces—those who fly about at night having become birds, or those who have placed their hostility toward the divine sacrifice.
Roll forth from heaven the stone, O Indra; O Maghavan, sharpen it, whetted by Soma.
From the east, from the west, from below, and from above, strike down the demons with the mountain! 19.
(8.4.20) These very dog-demons fly about; seeking to harm, they wish to deceive Indra, the undeceivable.
Śakra whets his weapon for the treacherous; he shall now hurl his thunderbolt at the sorcerers.
(8.4.21) Indra has become the destroyer of the sorcerers who plunder the oblation, as they seek to overpower him.
Let Śakra come upon the Rākṣasas, shattering them like an axe felling a forest, or like one breaking vessels. 21.
Slay the owl-demon, slay the screech-owl-demon, slay the dog-demon and the *kokaya* demon;
slay the eagle-demon and the vulture-demon—O Indra, crush the *rakṣas* like a millstone! 22.
Let no demon, nor any sorcerer, overcome us; let the paired Kimīdins be driven away.
May the earth protect us from earthly distress, and may the atmosphere protect us from celestial harm. //23//
O Indra, slay the male sorcerer and also the woman who exults in her magic power.
Let the fools who worship false gods perish with their necks broken; let them not behold the sun as it rises. 24.
Look back, look around; O Indra and Soma, remain awake!
Cast forth your weapon at the *rakṣas* demons, hurl your thunderbolt at the sorcerers!
This protective amulet, a hero, is bound upon the hero.
Possessing valor, a slayer of rivals, a heroic hero, a protector, and most auspicious. //1//
This amulet is the slayer of rivals, rich in heroes, powerful, victorious, and fierce; as a hero, it goes forth, destroying and turning back the sorcery.
With this amulet Indra slew Vṛtra; with this the wise one overcame the Asuras.
With this he conquered both these, heaven and earth; with this he conquered the four quarters. //3//
This amulet of Srāktya is a turner-back and a protection; powerful, subduing adversaries, and self-controlled, may it protect us on every side. //4//
This Agni has said, and Soma has said it; Bṛhaspati, Savitṛ, and Indra have said it.
May these gods, my domestic priests, drive back the sorceries with their counter-spells. //5//
I have placed between [myself and the enemy] heaven and earth, as well as day and the sun.
May those gods, acting as my domestic priests, drive back the sorceries with their counter-spells. //6//
Those people who make the *srāktya* amulet their armor—
having ascended to heaven like the sun— he, the controller, drives away the sorcery.
With the *srāktya* amulet, like a seer who is wise, I have conquered all hostile armies; I strike down the demons. //8//
The spells belonging to the Aṅgirases, the spells belonging to the Asuras,
the spells fashioned by oneself, and those brought by others—
let both these types go away to the far distance, beyond the ninety navigable rivers.
(8.5.10) May the gods—Indra, Viṣṇu, Savitṛ, Rudra, and Agni—bind this amulet as armor for him;
may Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, Virāj, Vaiśvānara, and all the ṛṣis [do so].
(8.5.11) You are the highest of plants, like the ox among moving creatures, and like the tiger among beasts of prey.
Him whom we sought, him we have found: the one who stands as our protector nearby.
He indeed becomes a tiger, and also a lion, and also a bull—
he who wears this amulet, the destroyer of rivals.
Neither Apsarases, nor Gandharvas, nor mortals slay him;
he who wears this amulet shines forth in all directions. 13.
Kaśyapa created you; Kaśyapa brought you together. Indra bore you among men, and bearing you, he conquered his adversaries.
The gods made this amulet of a thousandfold power their armor. 14.
Whoever seeks to strike you down with sorcery, with consecrations, or with sacrifices—
O Indra, turn against him and slay him with your hundred-jointed thunderbolt.
This indeed is the turning-back amulet, powerful and victorious;
may it protect our offspring and wealth, a secure defense and a source of great auspiciousness.
Make us free from rivals from below, free from rivals from above;
O Hero Indra, place light before us and make us free from rivals from behind.
May Heaven and Earth be my armor; may the Day be my armor, and the Sun my armor.
May Indra and Agni be my armor; may Dhātṛ bestow armor upon me. 18.

The armor belonging to Indra and Agni, which is thick and formidable, which none of all the gods can pierce through—that may protect my body on every side, so that I may be long-lived and reach old age. 19.
The divine amulet has ascended unto me for great safety; enter into this pillar, which protects the body and provides triple defense for the sake of vigor.
In this [child], may Indra bestow manly vigor; O gods, enter into him!
So that he may live a long life of a hundred autumns, may he be long-lived and reach old age. 21.
Bestower of well-being, lord of the people, slayer of Vṛtra, dispeller of foes,
the controller— Indra, the victorious and unconquered, the Soma-drinker who grants fearlessness and is the bull, shall bind this amulet for you.
Those two who cleansed you, mother, when you were born—the finders of a husband—let not the ill-named one there covet you, nor the *aliṃśa*, nor the *vatsapa*. 1.
Palāla and Anupalāla, Śarku, Koka, Malimluca, and Palījaka; Āśreṣa, Vavrivāsas, Ṛkṣagrīva, and Pramīlin.
Do not be enveloped; do not creep toward me; do not creep between my thighs.
I prepare for her a remedy, a *baja* that drives away those of evil name.
The ill-named and the well-named, both desire what is enclosed;
we strike away the *arāya* demons; let the well-named one seek out the woman.
The black, hairy Asura who is rooted in the ground and has a snout—
him we drive away from her, along with the *arāya* worms, from her testicles and from her pubic region.
The brown *baja* has destroyed the *arāya*, the *śvakiṣkin*, and the one who sniffs, the one who feels about, the flesh-eater, and the one who licks his lips.
Whoever lies with you in sleep, having become like a brother or like a father—
let the *baja* strike him away from here, those who have the form of eunuchs and wear turbans.
He who creeps toward you while you sleep, he who seeks to harm you while you are awake— just as the sun, moving around it, destroys the shadow, so has he destroyed them.
O herb, destroy that man who makes this woman bear a dead child or one that miscarries— him who is as slippery as a lotus stalk.
Those who dance around the houses at evening, braying like donkeys;
those who are *kusūlas*, *kukṣilas*, *kakubhas*, *karumas*, and *srimas*—O Herb, destroy them with your fragrance, scattering them in all directions. 10. {14}
Those who have goiters, those with scrofulous swellings, who wear skins and rags;
those who, like eunuchs, dance about and make a clamor in the forest—them we cause to perish from here. //11//
Those who cannot endure the sun as it scorches yonder from heaven—those *arāya* worms dwelling in sheepskins, the foul-smelling, red-mouthed *makaka*s—we cause them to perish. 12.
O Indra, destroy the *rakṣas* who carry themselves excessively upon their shoulders, and who strike the hips of women with their goads. 13.

Those who go forward as bridegrooms, bearing horns in their hands, those who stay at the hearth, those who laugh aloud, and those who produce light in the sacrificial post—those we cause to perish from here. 14.
Those whose heels are behind, whose heels are in front, whose faces are in front;
those born from chaff, born from dung-smoke, the *uruṇḍas* and the *maṭmaṭas*, those with pot-like testicles and those who are sluggish—O Brahmaṇaspati, destroy them with this awakening spell! 15.
Let them have rolling eyes, let them be unable to walk, let them be without women—let them be eunuchs.
O healing herb, cast down him who seeks to deprive this woman of her husband while she has her own lord. 16.
The one with bristling hair, the one with matted locks, the one who crushes, the one who rubs;
the approaching one, the copper-colored, the snout-like, and the *śāluḍa*—
pierce them with your foot and your heel, as a bull kicks over a water-pot!
Whoever should touch your embryo, or kill you once born—
may Piṅga, with his formidable bow, pierce him to the heart.
Those who kill those born from the womb and lie in wait for women in childbirth—let Piṅga drive away these Gandharvas belonging to the female class, as the wind drives away the clouds. 19.
May that which has been wiped away hold fast; may it not fall upon me.
May the two fierce ones, the healers who wear their garments as a girdle, protect your embryo—from the *pavīnasa*, from the *taṅgalva*, from the *śāyaka*, and even from the *nagnaka*.
For offspring and for the husband, let the tawny one protect you from the Kimīdins. //21//
From the two-faced, four-eyed, five-footed, fingerless one,
from the stalk that creeps forth and rolls about— protect us from it!
Those who eat raw flesh and those who eat the bloody flesh of men,
the long-haired ones who devour fetuses— these we cause to perish from here.
Those who creep away from the sun like a daughter-in-law from her father-in-law— let Bāja and Piṅga pierce them through the heart.
O Piṅga, protect the one being born; let them not make [him] a man or a woman.
Let the egg-eaters not harm the embryos; drive away these Kimīdins from here! 25.
Childlessness, the death of offspring, weeping, misfortune, and distress—
having fashioned these like a garland from a tree, cast them upon the one you dislike.
Those that are brown, those that are bright, those that are ruddy, and those that are speckled.
We call upon all the black and dark plants. //1//
May they protect this man from the consumption sent by the gods—
those plants of whom heaven is the father, earth the mother, and the ocean has become the root.
The waters are the first of the divine herbs;
may they destroy from limb by limb the consumption and the sin that is yours.
Spreading out, forming clumps, and growing single-stemmed shoots, I invoke the spreading plants;
those that are fibrous and thorny, those with many branches—I call upon these herbs belonging to all the gods, formidable, and the sustainers of men. 4.
O conquering plants, whatever subduing power is yours, and whatever strength is yours—with that, O plants, release this man from this consumption; thus do I prepare a remedy. //5//
The life-giving, the inviolable, the living herb— I here invoke Arundhatī, the up-lifter, the flowering, the honey-sweet, for his safety.
May those who are wise come hither to my words,
so that we may carry this man across from distress.
The food of Agni, the embryo of the waters, those plants that grow ever anew—
may these herbs, steadfast and bearing a thousand names, be healing when brought hither.
The plants, whose essence is water and which contain the *avakā*,
let loose their evil with their sharp points.
Those fierce plants that release from the bonds of Varuṇa, those that neutralize poison,
and those that destroy the seat of *balāsa* and corrupt magical spells— may those herbs come here.
The most powerful creepers, purchased and praised, [are here].
May they protect the cow, the horse, the man, and the livestock in this village. //11//
Sweet is their root, sweet is their tip; sweet has become the middle of these plants.
Sweet is their leaf, sweet is their flower; may they, as sharers of honey and consumers of nectar, yield for us clarified butter as food, with the cow as the leader.
However many and of whatever kind these plants are upon the earth— may they, with their thousand leaves, release me from death and from distress.
The tiger-skin amulet, the protector among plants, which guards against curses—may it drive away all diseases and demons far from us. 14.
They tremble before them as before the roar of a lion; they flee from them as before a fire brought near.
May the consumption of cattle and men, driven away by these plants, pass into the navigable rivers.
The plants, being released from Agni Vaiśvānara, come hither spreading over the earth— those of whom the Lord of the Forest is the king.
Those plants of the Aṅgirases that grow upon the mountains and upon the level plains—may those plants be full of milk and auspicious for us, bringing peace to our hearts. 17.
Those plants which I know, and those which I see with my eyes—
those unknown and those we do know, and in which we recognize that which is gathered.
May all the herbs together heed my words,
so that we may deliver this man from misfortune.
The *aśvattha* tree, the *darbha* grass, Soma the king among plants, the immortal oblation;
rice and barley are the two medicines, the two immortal sons of Heaven.
You lift yourselves up; you thunder and you roar, O plants.
When Parjanya bestows seed upon you, O sons of Pṛśni. //21//
With this nectar, we cause this man to drink strength;
moreover, I prepare a remedy so that he may live for a hundred autumns.
The boar knows the plant; the mongoose knows the healing herb.
Those which the serpents and the Gandharvas know, those I invoke for his protection. 23.
Those *oṣadhi*s that the fair-winged ones of Aṅgiras know, those that the celestial *raghata*s know, those that the birds, the swans, and all winged creatures know,
and those that the wild beasts know— those I summon for his protection. 24.
As many herbs as cows, the inviolable ones, eat, and as many as goats and sheep;
so many herbs, once brought here, shall grant you protection. 25.
As many medicinal plants as physicians know among mankind,
so many all-healing herbs do I bring hither for you.
May those that are flowering, those that have blossomed, those that bear fruit, and those that are fruitless—
may they all yield for him, like mothers together, for his safety.
I have drawn you forth from the five-fold [net], and also from the ten-fold;
and also from the fetter of Yama, and from every sin against the gods. May Indra churn [thee] forth, the churning one, the powerful, the hero, the breaker of forts.
So that we may strike down the armies of our enemies by the thousands. //1//
Let the foul-smelling rope, used for blowing [the fire], make that army foul;
let them see the smoke and the fire from afar, and let fear be placed in the hearts of the enemies.
O Aśvattha tree, crush those men; O Khadira, devour them! Let them break like a sudden fracture; let the executioner slay them with his weapons.
May those called *paruṣāhva* make those enemies rough; may the slayer strike them down with his weapons.
May they quickly break apart like arrows, bound together by a great net.
The atmosphere was the net; the great quarters of space were the poles of the net.
With that, Śakra, having enveloped the Dasyus, scattered their army. 5.
For great is the net of the mighty Śakra, the possessor of the prize;
with it, press down upon all enemies so that not even one of them may escape.
Great is your net, O great Indra, hero of a thousandfold value and hundredfold prowess.
With it, Śakra, having assailed the Dasyus with his army, slew a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, and a hundred million.
This great world was the net of the mighty Śakra;
with that net of Indra, I shroud all these people in darkness.
Exhaustion, fierce failure, and incurable affliction, as well as fatigue, lassitude, and delusion—with these I overwhelm them all. 9.
I deliver these to Death; they are bound by the snares of Death. Those who are the malevolent messengers of Death—to them I lead these away, having bound them.
(10) O messengers of Death, lead these away! O messengers of Yama, hold them back!
Let more than a thousand be slain; let them trample these [enemies] down, O mortal Bhava! 11.
The Sādhyas go forth with might, raising up one net-pole;
the Rudras [raise] one, the Vasus one, and it is raised by the Ādityas as one. 12.
May all the gods go above, pressing down with their might; may the Aṅgirases go through the middle, striking down the great army. 13.
The lords of the forest, the products of the forest, the herbs, and the plants—I dispatch the bipeds and quadrupeds so that they may slay that army. 14.
The Gandharvas, Apsarases, serpents, gods, holy folk, and ancestors—whether seen or unseen—I impel them so that they may slay that army. 15.
(8.8.16a) These death-traps have been sown, treading upon which you shall not be released.
(8.8.16c) May this snare of that army be destroyed by the thousands! 16.
The cauldron is kindled by fire; this offering brings a thousandfold reward.
O Bhava and Pṛśnibāhu, and Śarva, destroy that army! 17.
Let them fall into the mouth of death, into hunger, exhaustion, slaughter, and fear!
O Indra and Śarva, with your nets of eyes, strike down that army! 18
Let the enemies, utterly defeated, tremble; driven away, run off by the sacred word (*brahman*).
Of those who have been driven away by Bṛhaspati, let no one whatsoever escape me. 19.
May their weapons fall down; may they not be able to fix an arrow to the string.
Then, as they are greatly terrified, let their arrows strike their vital organs. 20.
Let Heaven and Earth cry out against them, along with the intermediate space and the deities!
Let them find neither a kinsman nor a firm support; striking one another down, let them go unto death. 21.
The four quarters are the mares of the divine chariot; the sacrificial cakes are the hooves, and the intermediate space is the axle-socket.
Heaven and earth are the two side-pieces, the seasons are the reins, the intermediate directions are the attendants, and speech is the chariot-rail.

The *saṃvatsara* is the chariot, the *parivatsara* is the seat of the chariot, the *virāj* is the pole, and Agni is the front of the chariot; Indra is the driver on the left, and the Moon is the charioteer. //23//
From here conquer, from there conquer, conquer completely; conquer, svāhā!
Let these conquer, let those yonder be conquered, svāhā!
From these [beings] and from those evil ones, I strike them down with dark-blue and red [poison]. 24. {21}
From where were those two born? Which is that half? From what world, from which earth?
The two calves of Virāj rose up from the ocean; I ask you about them: by which one were they milked?
He who, lying upon his triple-folded womb, caused the waters to roar by his greatness—
he, the calf of Virāj, the yielder of desires, made his bodies secret in the far distance.
Those three which are great, of which one separates the fourth as speech—let the wise man, through austerity, know that Brahman in which the one is joined, in which the one is joined. //3//
From the *bṛhat* [sāman], the *sāmans* were fashioned; from the sixth, the five were fashioned. The *bṛhat* was fashioned from the *bṛhatī*; from what was the *bṛhatī* measured out? //4//
The Bṛhatī has been fashioned from the measure of the mother, beyond the mother’s measure;
indeed, Māyā was born from Māyā, and from Māyā came Mātali.
The image of Vaiśvānara is above the sky; as far as the two worlds extend, so far Agni prevails.
From there, from that sixth [day] beyond, the hymns proceed; from here they go forth toward the sixth day.

We six seers, O Kaśyapa, ask you this, for you indeed join together what is joined and what is to be joined. They call Virāj the father of Brahman; bestow her upon us, your friends, in as many ways as there are.

She, following whom the sacrifices fall away when she falls away, and who they attend when she attends; she in whose ordinance and impulse the spirit moves—that Virāj, O seers, is in the highest heaven.
Breathing not with breath among those who breathe, the Virāj follows after the self-ruling Svarāj.
Some behold her as the all-touching, well-formed Virāj; others do not behold her.
Who knows the state of union of Virāj? Who knows her seasons, and who her ritual order? Who knows her steps, how manyfold they have been milked? Who knows her abodes, and how manyfold her dawns?
This is she who first shone forth; she moves, having entered into these other [dawns].
Great are the glories within her; the bride, the ninefold mother, has won them.
In the wing of the *chandas*, the two Dawns, beautifully adorned, move together toward a common womb.
As wives of the Sun, they move together, wise, conscious, undecaying, and possessed of abundant seed. 12.
Three have followed the path of *ṛta*; three heats have followed the seed.
One quickens progeny, one [quickens] vigor, and one protects the kingdom of those who seek the gods. 13.

Agni and Soma established those which were the fourth part when the seers, fashioning the two wings of the sacrifice, brought forth for the sacrificer the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, the Anuṣṭubh, and the Bṛhadarkī, which brings the light of heaven. 14.
Five dawns follow the five milkings; the seasons follow the cow of five names.
The five directions are fashioned by the fifteenfold [stoma]; they have a single summit toward the one world. 15.
Six are the beings born, the first-born of Cosmic Order; six indeed are the *sāman* chants that carry the six-day sacrifice.
Six yokes they say follow the plow for every *sāman*; there are six heavens and earths, six wide expanses.
They say there are six cold months and six hot months; tell us which season is the extra one.
Seven wise birds have sat down; seven meters follow, and seven initiations.
Seven are the oblations, seven indeed the fuel-sticks, seven the honeys, and seven the seasons.
Seven offerings of clarified butter have encompassed all that exists; we have heard them called the "seven vultures. 18.
The seven meters, each increasing by four syllables, are superposed one upon another.
How do the *stomas* find their support in them? And how are they superposed within those *stomas*? //19//
(20a) How did the Gāyatrī pervade the Trivṛt? How does the Triṣṭubh correspond with the Pañcadaśa?
(20c) How does the Jagatī [correspond] with the Trayastriṃśa, and how the Anuṣṭubh with the Ekaviṃśa?
{23} (21a) Eight are the beings born first from the *ṛta*, O Indra; eight are the divine officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Aditi has eight wombs and eight sons; toward her on this eighth night, the oblation goes forth.
Thinking this to be better, I have come here; I am auspicious in your friendship.
Your *kratu*-intention is of common origin and is propitious; knowing all, it moves among you all. 22.
Eight [streams] for Indra, six for Yama, seven for the seers in seven ways;
those waters have flowed following the five classes of men and the plants.
The young cow, yielding her first milk, has indeed yielded for the sole Lord the *vaśā* and the *pīyūṣa*;
then she satisfied the fourfold gods, humans, *asuras*, and *ṛṣis*.
Who indeed is the cow? Who is the sole seer? What is the abode? What are the blessings? That which on earth is the sole increaser, the sole season—what indeed is it? 25.
(8.9.26) One ox, one [sacrificer], one seer, one abode, and single-fold blessings;

the Yakṣa on earth, increasing by one, as the sole season, does not exceed [them]. (26) {24} (8.10.1) Virāj indeed was this in the beginning. When she was born, everything was afraid, thinking: "She alone will become all this. (1)
She stepped forth; she stepped down into the *gārhapatya* fire.
He who knows thus becomes a master of the household, a lord of the house. //2//
He stepped forth; he stepped down into the *sāhavanīya* fire.
The gods go to his invocation of the gods; he becomes dear to the gods, who knows thus. //3//
She stepped forth; she stepped down into the southern fire.
He who knows thus becomes one who is eager for sacrifice, worthy of sacrificial gifts, and a recipient of a guest-offering. 4.
She stepped forth; she stepped down into the assembly hall.
He who knows thus goes to his assembly hall and becomes a member of the assembly. //5//
She stepped forth; she stepped down into the assembly.
Those who know thus go to his assembly; he becomes one who belongs to the assembly.
He stepped forth; he stepped down into the place of invocation.
He who knows this becomes one worthy of invocation, for they come to his invocation.
//7// He stepped forth; he stood having stepped out fourfold into the intermediate space. //8//
The gods and humans said to her: "She alone knows that by which we both may subsist; let us invoke her."
They called out to her. //10//
"Come, O strength! Come, O svadhā! Come, O truth! Come, O you who possess nourishment! //11//
Indra was her calf; the Gāyatrī was the rope around her neck; the cloud was her udder. //12//
The Bṛhat and the Rathantara were his two breasts; the Yajñāyajñīya and the Vāmadevya were the other two. 13.
By means of the Rathantara, the gods milked the plants; by means of the Bṛhat, they milked the expanse.
One should offer water with the Vāmadevya hymn and the sacrifice with the Yajñāyajñīya. //15//
Verily, for him the plants milk forth the Rathantara and the Bṛhat as wide space.
He who knows the waters, the Vāmadevya, the sacrifice, and the Yajñāyajñīya—[he prospers].
She stepped forth; she went to the trees. The trees struck her down. She came together again within a year.
Therefore, what is cut from the trees grows back again after a year. He who knows this cuts off his hostile rival.
She stepped forth; she went to the Pitṛs. The Pitṛs struck her down; she became the month.
Therefore, they offer the Upamāsyam [oblation] to the Pitṛs in the month. He who knows thus knows the path traveled by the Pitṛs. //19//
She stepped forth; she went to the gods. The gods slew her; she became [the moon] in the half-month.
Therefore, they utter *vaṣaṭ* to the gods in the half-month. He who knows thus knows the path that leads to the gods. //20//
She stepped forth; she came to the humans. The humans killed her, and she immediately became pregnant.
Therefore, they offer [food] to humans on alternate days; they bring it to the house of one who knows thus.
She stepped forth; she came to the Asuras. The Asuras called out to her, "O Māyā, come!"
Virocana, the son of Prahrādi, was her calf; an iron vessel was her milk-pail.
Dvimūrdhan, the son of Ṛtvi, milked her; he milked her as a magical power (*māyā*).
The Asuras subsist upon that illusion; he who knows this becomes one upon whom others must subsist. //22//
She stepped forth; she went to the ancestors. The ancestors called out to her: "O Svadhā, come!
King Yama was her calf, and her vessel was a silver bowl.
Antaka Mārtyava milked her; he milked that very Svadhā.
The ancestors live upon that *svadhā*; he who knows this becomes one who is to be lived upon. //23//
She stepped forth; she came to human beings. Human beings called out to her, "O possessor of refreshment, come! Manu Vaivasvata was her calf, and the earth was her vessel.
Pṛthī Vainya milked her; he milked from her both agriculture and grain.
Upon them humans depend for their *svadhā*, for their cultivation, and for their crops; he who knows this becomes one whose success in agriculture is the means of his livelihood. 24.
She stepped forth; she went to the Seven Seers. The Seven Seers called out to her, "O you who possess the sacred word (*brahman*), come! King Soma was her calf, and the meter was her vessel.
Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa milked her; he milked from her both the sacred word and ascetic heat (*tapas*).
(25) That *brahman* and that austerity the Seven Seers live upon; he who knows this becomes one who lives upon the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*), one who is to be lived upon.
(26) She stepped forth; she went to the gods. The gods called out to her: "O Food, come! Indra was her calf, and the cup was her vessel.
The god Savitṛ has bestowed that; he has bestowed that very strength.
The gods live upon that strength; he who knows thus becomes one to be lived upon. 26.

She stepped forth; she went toward the Gandharvas and Apsarases. The Gandharvas and Apsarases called out to her, "O you of holy fragrance, come! Citraratha Sauryavarcas was her calf, and a lotus leaf was her vessel.
Vasuruci Sauryavarcas milked her; he milked from her only holy fragrance.
The Gandharvas and Apsarases subsist upon that meritorious fragrance; he who knows this becomes one of meritorious fragrance, worthy of being subsisted upon. //27//
She stepped forth; she went beyond the common folk, and the common folk called out to her, "Hide away!
Come! Kubera Vaiśravaṇa was her calf, and an unbaked earthen vessel was her bowl.
Kaberaka, whose navel was silver, milked her; he milked her right there where she had hidden.
The ancestors live upon that which has been made to vanish beyond the dust; he who knows this makes all evil vanish and becomes one upon whom others depend for their livelihood. //28//
She stepped forth; she came to the serpents. The serpents called out to her, "Come, O Poisonous One!
Takṣaka Vaiśaleya was her calf, and an alābu gourd was her vessel.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra Airāvata milked her; he milked only poison.
All depend upon that poison for their livelihood; he who knows this becomes one upon whom others depend for their livelihood. 29.
If one were to consecrate such a knower with a gourd, it would strike back at him. 30.
One should not strike back; however, one may strike back with the thought, "I am striking you with my mind. //31//
Whatever poison one strikes back, that very poison one strikes back. //32//
Poison indeed is poured upon his hostile rival who knows this.
From heaven, from earth, from the intermediate space, from the ocean, from fire, and from the winds, the honey-plant was born.
All creatures welcome her with their hearts as she comes, clothed in immortality.
Great is her milk, multiform; they say it is the seed of the ocean.
From where the honey-whip comes forth, bestowing gifts—therein is breath, therein is the immortal established.
Men on earth, investigating in many ways, behold her various movements;
for from Agni and the winds was born Madhukasha, the fierce granddaughter of the Maruts.

The mother of the Ādityas, the daughter of the Vasus, the breath of creatures, the navel of immortality—she of golden hue, the honeyed stalk, dripping with clarity, the great splendor moves among mortals. //4//
The gods produced a whip from honey; its embryo became the one of all forms.
The mother nourishes him when he is born and young; once born, he gazes upon all beings. //5//
Who knows him, and who has perceived him—he who is the inexhaustible jar of Soma within her heart? May the wise Brahman rejoice in this.
He knows those two, and he perceives them—the two inexhaustible breasts of this [Earth] that flow in a thousand streams;
yielding nourishment, they milk without ceasing.
Making the sound *hiṅ*, the great bestower of vitality, she approaches her vow with a loud cry;
lowing toward the three heats, she utters her lowing and yields milk with her milks.
The waters that sit upon the swelling [cloud], those Śākvara bulls who are self-sovereign—they rain down;
they cause to rain. For him who knows this, the waters fulfill his desire and provide nourishment.
(9.1.10a) Your voice, O Prajāpati, is the thunder; as a bull, you cast forth vigor upon the earth.
(9.1.10c) For from Agni and the winds was born the honey-whip, the fierce granddaughter of the Maruts.
(9.1.11a) Just as Soma is dear to the Aśvins at the morning pressing, so [be this] for us.
Even so, O Aśvins, may splendor be established within my self. //11//
Just as Soma is dear to Indra and Agni at the second pressing, even so may splendor be maintained within my own self by Indra and Agni. 12.
Just as Soma is dear to the Ṛbhus at the third pressing, even so, O Ṛbhus, may splendor be established within my own self. 13.
May I be born of honey; may I win honey.
Rich in milk, O Agni, have I come; unite me with splendor. //14//
O Agni, unite me with splendor, unite me with progeny, and unite me with long life.
May the gods take note of this for me; may Indra, together with the seers, take note.
Just as honey-makers collect honey upon the honeycomb, even so, O Aśvins, may splendor be established within my self. 16.
Just as bees smear this honey upon the honeycomb, even so, O Aśvins, may splendor, brilliance, strength, and vital power be maintained within me. 17.
Whatever honey is in the hills, in the mountains, in the cows, and in the horses; whatever honey is in the surā being poured out—may that honey be in me. 18.
O Aśvins, lords of splendor, anoint me with the honey of the bee, so that I may utter speech full of luster among the people. 19.19
(9.1.20a) Your voice, O Prajāpati, is the thunder; as a bull, you cast forth vigor upon the earth and in the sky.
(9.1.20c) All creatures depend upon that for life; by it, he nourishes this food and strength. //20//
The earth is the staff, the intermediate space is the embryo, the sky is the whip, lightning is the lash, and the golden drop is the tip. //21//
Whoever knows the seven honeyed products of the *kaśā* becomes possessed of honey:
the Brahmin, the King, the milch-cow, the ox, rice, barley, and honey as the seventh. 22.
It becomes honeyed; its food-offering becomes honeyed.
He who knows this conquers honeyed worlds. //23//
When it thunders in a cloudless sky, Prajāpati himself manifests for his creatures.
Therefore, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, one should stand and say: "O Prajāpati, wake up after me!
Those who know this, Prajāpati wakes up after them, and so do their offspring. 24. {2}
I honor with ghee, oblation, and clarified butter the bull that slays rivals, so that my desire may be fulfilled.
Being praised with great heroic power, do you trample my rivals beneath my feet. 1.
Whatever is not dear to my mind, whatever my eye consumes but does not welcome—that evil dream I cast back upon my rival; having praised my desire, may I shatter him.
O Kāma, cast upon him the evil dream, misfortune, childlessness, homelessness, and distress—upon that fierce lord who seeks to harm us with affliction. (AVŚ 9.2.3)
Drive them away, O Kāma; drive them far away, O Kāma! Let those who are my rivals go to ruin.
When they have been driven down into the lowest darkness, O Agni, do you utterly burn up their dwellings.
O Kāma, she who is called Speech by the seers as the Virāj is said to be your daughter, the cow. With her, exclude my rivals; let breath, cattle, and life turn away from them. (5)
By the power of Kāma, Indra, and King Varuṇa, by the strength of Viṣṇu and the impulse of Savitṛ,
and by the office of Agni as Hotṛ, may I drive away my rivals, just as a skillful steersman drives a boat upon the waters.
May my fierce and powerful steed, the overseer, make me truly free from rivals.
May all the gods be my protectors; may all the gods come to this invocation of mine.
Enjoying this clarified butter mixed with ghee, you who have desire as your chief, rejoice here, making me truly free from rivals. //8//
O Indra and Agni, having mounted the same chariot at my desire, cast down my rivals;
once they have fallen into the lowest darkness, O Agni, do you burn up their dwellings. 9.
Slay, O Kāma, those who are my rivals; cast them down into blind darkness.
Let them all be deprived of their senses and tasteless; let not even a single day of their lives remain. Kāma has slain those who were my rivals; he has made for me a wide world of prosperity.
May the four quarters bow down to me; may the six wide expanses bring me clarified butter.
Let them float downward, like a ship severed from its moorings;
for those driven away by arrows, there is no returning again. 12.
Agni is the *yava*, Indra is the *yava*, Soma is the *yava*; may the gods, the *yavayāvāna*s, drive him away. //13//
May he wander about, deprived of all his heroes, driven away, hated by his friends, and cast out by his own kin.
And may the lightnings descend upon him on the earth; may the fierce god crush your rivals. 14.
This *bṛhatī* has fallen, yet it is unfallen; it bears the lightning and all the thunders.
Rising with wealth and splendor, may the powerful Āditya push my rivals down. 15.

O Kāma, that triple-layered protection of yours which has arisen, that *brahman*-shield fashioned as impenetrable and spread abroad—with that, exclude my rivals; let breath, cattle, and life itself avoid them. (AVŚ 9.2.16)
With that by which the gods repelled the Asuras, and with which Indra drove the Dasyus into the lowest darkness—with that, O Kāma, drive far away from this world those who are my rivals. 17.
Just as the gods drove away the Asuras, and just as Indra forced the Dasyus into the lowest darkness, so do you, O Kāma, drive far away from this world those who are my rivals. 18.
Desire was born first; neither the gods, nor the ancestors, nor mortals have reached its limit.
Therefore, you are greater and forever great; to you, O Desire, I pay homage. //19//
As wide as heaven and earth are in their extent, as far as the waters flow, as far as fire reaches—greater than all that you are, forever great; to you, O Kāma, I offer my homage.
As many as are the quarters and the intermediate directions, spreading out in all ways, as many as are the regions visible from heaven.
Therefore you are superior and ever great; to you, O Kāma, I offer this homage. //21//
As many as there are bees, bats, and kurūravas; as many as there are vadhās and tree-serpents have become—greater than all those you are, forever great; to you, O Kāma, I thus offer homage. 22.
(9.2.23a) You are greater than that which blinks, you are greater than that which stands still, O Kāma, you are greater than the ocean, O Manyu.
(9.2.23c) Therefore, you are greater and ever-mighty; to you, O Kāma, I offer this homage. //23//
Truly, not even the wind attains its desire, nor Agni, nor the Sun, nor even the Moon;
therefore, you are greater and always more mighty than they. To you, O Kāma, I offer my salutation. //24//
(9.2.25a) Those auspicious forms of yours, O Kāma, which are blessed, by which that which you choose becomes true— (9.2.25c) with those do you enter into us; drive away evil thoughts elsewhere.
{5} (9.3.1a) That which is measured out, that which is counter-measured, and also that which is fully measured—
We unbind the fastenings of the hall that contains all desirable things. //1//
Whatever has been bound upon you, O Viśvavārā, whatever fetter and knot has been made—
like Bṛhaspati, I loosen that with my word.
He stretched it out, he tore it apart, and he made its knots firm;
as one who knows the joints, we loosen them with Indra, like a skilled reciter. 3.3.3a-c.
The bindings of your bamboo poles, the lashings of your leather thongs, and the cords of your straw— O Viśvavārā, we loosen all those fastenings of your wings.
The tongs, the straw-bundles, and the binding-thongs—
these fetters of Māna’s wife we now unloose.
Those loops within your sling that they fastened for the sake of sport—those we loosen for you. O Mistress of the Mind, be auspicious and helpful to our bodies when you have been raised up.
The oblation-holder, the fire-hall, the seat of the wives, and the assembly hall— O divine house, you are the assembly hall of the gods.
The thousand-eyed net, stretched out as a head-ornament at the zenith,
bound and fastened with a sacred prayer— we loosen it apart.
O House, may both he who accepts you and he by whom you were measured—
both of them, O Mistress of the Mansion, live to reach old age.
May it come to him from there— firmly bound, well-adorned—
that one of yours whose limbs you loosen, limb by limb, joint by joint. O House, he who built you together has gathered the lords of the forest.
For the sake of progeny, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati made you, O house, his own. //11//
Homage to him; we offer homage to the Giver and to the Lord of the House.
Homage to Agni as he moves forth, and homage to you, O Puruṣa. 12.
Homage to the cows, to the horses, and to that which is born in the stall; O prolific one, O mother of offspring, we loosen your snares. 13.
You conceal Agni within [the house] together with men and cattle;
O you who have offspring, who have progeny, we loosen your snares. 14.

With that expanse which lies between heaven and earth, with that I accept this hall for you. That which is the intermediate space, the measure of the region, that I make into a belly for the treasures;
with that I accept the hall for him. 15.
Full of vigor, full of milk, established and measured upon the earth—O house, bearing all kinds of food, do not harm those who receive you. 16.
Covered with grass, clad in straw, like the night, the hall is the resting place for all that moves;
measured upon the earth, you stand like a female elephant with feet. 17.
I unfasten for you what is fastened, uncovering that which was covered;
may Mitra unbind at dawn that which was pressed down by Varuṇa. 18.
The hall built by Brahmā, built by the seers, and measured out—may Indra and Agni protect that hall; may the two immortals protect the Soma-dwelling. 19.19a-c.
Nest within nest, sheath within sheath is gathered together;
therein the mortal is born, from whom all is produced.
(20) She who is fashioned with two wings, four wings, or six wings— (21)
In the hall with eight sides or ten sides, the mistress of the dwelling, Agni lies like an embryo.
Facing westward, O house, I approach you who are facing westward and are non-violent;
for within you are fire and waters—the first gate of Cosmic Order (*ṛta*).
I bring forth these waters, free from disease and destroyers of disease;
I settle into my home together with Agni, the immortal.
Do not cast a snare upon us; let the heavy burden become light.
O house, we carry you wherever we desire, as if you were a bride. 24.
From the eastern direction, from the hall, homage to the Greatness; Svāhā to the gods, Svāhā to those worthy of Svāhā! //25//
To the southern direction, to the hall, homage to its greatness! Svāhā! To the gods who are to be honored with svāhā! //26//
From the western direction, from the hall, homage to the Greatness; Svāhā! To the gods who are to be invoked with Svāhā! //27//
From the northern direction, from the hall, homage to the Greatness; Svāhā! To the gods who are to be invoked with Svāhā! //28//
To the firm quarter, to the hall, homage to its greatness! Svāhā to the gods, svāhā to those worthy of svāhā! //29//
To the hall from the upward direction, homage to its greatness! Svāhā to the gods, svāhā to those worthy of svāhā! //30//
To every direction of the hall, homage to its greatness! Svāhā to the gods, svāhā to those worthy of oblations!

This thousandfold, brilliant bull, rich in milk, bearing all forms within his flanks—he, the son of Bṛhaspati, the ruddy one, stretching out the thread of the sacrifice, bestows prosperity upon the donor and the sacrificer.

He who has become the counterpart of the waters, O Agni, the master over all like the Goddess Earth—may he, the father of calves and the lord of the cows, grant us prosperity consisting of a thousandfold increase. 2.
A male, pregnant, ancient, and full of milk—the bull bears the vessel of wealth.
May Agni Jātavedas carry him, offered as an oblation, to Indra by the paths traveled by the gods. 3.
Father of the calves, lord of the cows, and father of the great jars;
the calf, the afterbirth, the fresh milk, the cream, the curd, and the clarified butter—this indeed is his seed. //4//
This is the portion of the gods, this is the grudge, the essence of the waters, of the plants, and of the clarified butter.
Śakra chose the draught of Soma; that which was his body became the great pressing-stone.
You bear a jar filled with Soma; you are Tvaṣṭṛ, the fashioner of forms and the progenitor of cattle.
May these wombs here be auspicious for us; O Svadhiti, hold fast those that are near and those that are far away.
He bears the goat; clarified butter is his seed; he is a thousandfold nourishment—him they call the sacrifice.
The bull, wearing the form of Indra, may he come to us as a gracious gift, O gods. 7.

The vigor of Indra, the two arms of Varuṇa, the shoulders of the Aśvins, and this hump of the Maruts—this [body] they call Bṛhaspati once he has been fully formed, those who are wise, seers, and possessed of insight. //8//
(9a) You, rich in milk, extend yourself to the divine clans; they call you Indra, they call you Sarasvant.
(9c) He who, being a Brahmin, offers up a bull as a sacrifice bestows a thousand [cows] with a single mouth. //9//
Bṛhaspati and Savitṛ have bestowed vital strength upon you; from Tvaṣṭṛ and Vāyu, your very self has been brought hither.
With my mind, I offer you into the intermediate space; may both Heaven and Earth be your sacrificial grass.
(10) He who goes among the cattle, lowing loudly like Indra among the gods— (11a)
May Brahmā praise the limbs of that bull with auspiciousness.
The two sides were Anumati’s; the two thighs were Bhaga’s.
Mitra said of the two knee-bones: "These belong to me alone."
The buttocks were of the Ādityas; the hips were of Bṛhaspati;
the tail was of the god Vāta; with it he shakes the plants. //13//
They said the intestines belonged to Sinīvālī; they said the skin belonged to Sūryā.
They said the footprint belonged to Utthātṛ, when they fashioned the bull. 14.
The breast was that of Jāmiśaṃsa; the Soma-pressing vessel was held firm, when all the gods, having come together, fashioned the bull. 15.
They gave the humps to Saramā and the hooves to the tortoises; they set aside his undigested food for the worms that turn like dogs.
With his two horns the bull drives away the demon and destroys misfortune with his eye;
he who is the inviolable lord of cattle hears what is auspicious with his two ears. //17//
He performs a hundredfold sacrifice; the fires do not burn him.
All the gods quicken him who offers the bull to the Brahmin. 18.
Having given a bull to the Brahmins, he makes his mind more expansive;
he beholds the prosperity of his cows within his own pen.
May there be cattle, may there be progeny, and may there be bodily strength;
may the gods grant all that to the giver of the bull.
May this Indra, having drunk, bestow upon us conscious wealth;
may he, beyond the sky, milk for us the wise cow, well-yielding, ever accompanied by her calf, and granting all desires. 21.
Tawny-hued, bestowing vigor from the sky, the all-formed impetus of Indra has come to us.
Granting us long life and progeny, may he attend us with the increase of wealth. 22.
Come here, O Upapṛñcana; mingle us here in this cow-pen.
Mix us with the seed of the bull, O Indra, with your own heroic power.
(9.4.24a) We entrust this youth to you; sporting with him here, move according to your will.

(9.4.24c) Do not abandon us, O fortunate ones by birth; attend upon us with abundance of wealth. {10} (9.5.1a) Bring him here! Seize him! Let him go to the world of the doers of good deeds, knowing the way.
Having crossed through the many great darknesses, may the Unborn One ascend to the third heaven.
I lead you around as a portion for Indra, for the patron at this sacrifice, O wise one.
Seize those who hate us; may the heroes of the sacrificer be free from sin.
Wash away the tracks of whatever evil deed was committed; let him, knowing the way, step forward with pure hooves.
Having crossed over the darkness and seeing clearly in many ways, let the goat ascend to the third heaven, the firmament.

Having peeled this skin with a black knife, O dissector, do not think lightly of it as you cut it joint by joint with the sword. Do not harm it; fashion it limb by limb and place it upon the third heaven.
With a verse I place the pot upon the fire; pour out the water, set it down.
Enclose it with fire, O preparers; once cooked, let it go to the world where those of good deeds dwell. //5//
Ascend from here, if you have not been heated, above the heated cauldron to the third heaven.
You have become fire from the fire; conquer this world of light.
The goat is Agni; they say the light is the goat; they say the goat is to be given by the living man to the Brahman.
The goat drives away the darkness far away when it is given in this world by one who has faith. (AVŚ 9.5.7)
May the fivefold rice-offering, about to stride forth, step out in five ways toward the three lights.
Go to the midst of those who have sacrificed and performed good deeds; take your station upon the third firmament.
O goat, ascend to that world where the doers of good deeds dwell; like a śarabha, he shall not be cast down, but shall pass over all difficulties.
This five-rice-offering, when given to a Brahmin, shall satisfy the giver with full satisfaction. 9.
The goat places the giver upon the third heaven, the triple vault, on the back of the firmament.
The five-rice offering, when given to the Brahman, is one cow of all forms that milks every desire.
This is your third light, O Fathers; he gives the five-rice goat to the Brahman.
The goat, given by one who has faith in this world, drives away the darkness far away. (AVŚ 9.5.11c)
Desiring the world of those who have sacrificed and performed good deeds, he gives the five-fold rice-oblation to the Brahman;
may he conquer this world through pervasion, and may he, being auspicious, be accepted by us. 12.
For the goat was born from the heat of Agni; he is the sage of the sage, the wise one of strength.
May the gods, according to the seasons, ordain that which is sacrificed, bestowed, fully bestowed, and consecrated with the cry of *vaṣaṭ*. 13.
One should give unspun cloth and gold as a sacrificial fee;
thus one attains all the worlds, both those that are celestial and those that are terrestrial. 14.
(9.5.15a) May these divine streams, friendly to Soma, dripping with ghee and distilling honey, flow toward you.
(9.5.15c) Support the earth and the sky upon the back of the firmament, on the seven-rayed [vault]. 15.
(9.5.16a) You are the unborn; you are the unborn heaven. Through you, the Aṅgirases knew the world.
(9.5.16c) May I come to know that holy world. //16//
