O Agni, with that [power] by which you carry a thousand, and with which you carry all wealth—by that, carry this sacrifice of ours to the light, so that it may go among the gods. 17.
The cooked goat, the five-grain offering, repelling destruction, establishes one in the heavenly world;
through it, may we conquer the worlds possessed of the sun.

Whatever [portion] was placed with the Brahmins and whatever with the people, and whatever drops of the cooked rice of the goat—O Agni, may all that know us in the world of the well-done, at the meeting-place of the paths. 19.
O Agni, the Unborn indeed strode out across this [universe]; of him, this earth became the chest and the sky the back.
The intermediate space was his middle, the quarters were his sides, and the two oceans were his flanks.
(20) Truth and Order were his two eyes; the All is Truth, Faith is the breath, and the Virāj is the head. (21)
This indeed is the immeasurable sacrifice, namely the goat with five portions of rice.
He who gives a goat with five portions of cooked rice, having light as its sacrificial fee, attains an immeasurable sacrifice and secures for himself an immeasurable world.
One should not break his bones, nor should one extract the marrow;
taking him whole, one should cause him to enter this and that. 23.
This very form belongs to him; with it he unites him.
For him who gives a goat, the five-rice-dish, whose light is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), she milks out food, greatness, and vigor. //24//
Five gold ornaments, five new garments, and five cows that yield all desires belong to him who gives the goat with five portions of rice, whose light is the sacrificial fee.
Five golden ornaments become light for him; garments become armor for his body.
He who gives the five-porridge goat, whose light is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), attains the heavenly world. (AVŚ 9.5.26)
She who, having first found a husband, then finds another one after him—
may those two who give her a goat with five portions of rice not be separated.
He becomes a sharer of the same world with her who is born again, another husband, he who gives the goat that has five portions of rice and for which the sacrificial fee is light.
Having given a cow with a calf in due order, a draft-ox, a pillow, a garment, and gold, they go to the highest heaven.
I summon hither my own self, father, son, grandson, and grandfather; wife, progenitor, and mother—those who are dear to me.
O Naidāgha, he who indeed knows the season named Naidāgha...
This indeed is the season named Naidāgha, which is the goat with five portions of boiled rice.
It utterly burns away the splendor of the unpleasant rival; one prospers by oneself.
He who knows the season named Kurvat truly understands it.
As she acts, she indeed seizes away the fortune of the unpleasant rival.
This goat with five portions of rice is indeed the season named "Acting. He who knows the season named "Joining" [attains it].
(9.5.33c) He seizes the very splendor of his hostile rival, binding it again and again.
(9.5.33e) This goat with five portions of rice is indeed the season named Saṃyan.
(9.5.34a) Verily, he knows the season named Pinvant who [knows this].
Making her swell again and again, he takes away the fortune of his unpleasant rival.
This goat with five portions of rice is indeed the season named Pinvan.
He who knows the season named Udyant [the Rising]...
As it rises again and again, he takes away the fortune of the unpleasant rival.
Indeed, this season named "Rising" is the goat with five portions of rice.
Whoever knows the season named "Overpowering,"...
Overpowering, indeed overpowering, she takes away the fortune of the unpleasant rival.
This very season is indeed named Abhibhū (the Overpowerer), which is the goat with five portions of rice.
Cook the goat and the five portions of rice.
May all the quarters, being of one mind and united, together with the intermediate directions, receive this from you. //37//
(9.5.38a) May they protect you; for you, for your sake, I offer this clarified butter as an oblation to them.
//38// (9.6.1a) He who would know Brahman manifestly—he whose joints are the sacrificial materials, whose spine is the *ṛc* verses—//1//
The Sāmans are his body hairs; the Yajus is said to be his heart; the sacrificial strewing is indeed his oblation. 2.
Or when the host of guests looks upon the guests, he beholds the place of sacrifice to the gods. //3//
When he addresses [the officiant], he enters the consecration; when he asks for water, he leads forward the waters. //4//
Those very waters that are brought forward at the sacrifice are indeed those same ones. //5//
That libation which they bring, that very animal which is bound for Agni and Soma, is this one. //6//
When they prepare dwellings, they thereby prepare the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds. //7//
That which they spread out as a sacrificial grass-strew is indeed the *barhis*. //8//
When they bring a high bed, by that he wins the heavenly world. //9//
The coverlet and the mattress that they bring—these indeed are your enclosing-sticks.
When they bring collyrium and ointment, that is indeed clarified butter. //11//
Whatever they bring as a taste before the serving [of the meal], those two are indeed sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa). 12.
When they summon that which is caused by eating, they summon the preparer of the oblation itself. 13.
The rice and barley that are poured out are indeed the *aṃśu* stalks.
Those which are the mortars and pestles are indeed the pressing-stones.
The winnowing basket, the filter, the husks, the dregs, and the waters for pressing. //16//
The offering-ladle, the dipping-spoon, the stirring-stick, the mixing-vessel, the wooden troughs, the jars, the Vāyu-cups, and this very black antelope skin—
this is what the host of guests makes into a sacrificial manual for the patron when he looks at the things to be brought forward, saying, "Let this be more, let that be more!"
When he says, "Lift up further," he thereby makes his vital breath more extensive. //19//
He brings forward the oblations and sets them down. //20//
When they have approached, the guest offers himself as an oblation within them. 21.
With the ladle in his hand, he offers into the breath as the sacrificial post, with the *sruk* and the *vaṣaṭ* call. //22//
These indeed, both dear and not dear, are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); they cause [the host] to go to the heavenly world, namely the guests. 23.
He who, knowing this thus, does not eat while feeling hatred, nor eats the food of one who hates him, nor [eats] that of one who is suspected, nor of one who is currently suspecting [him]. 24.
Indeed, he whose food people eat has consumed all evil.
Indeed, everyone whose food others do not eat is one who has not consumed evil.

Or rather, he who offers [the oblation] is at all times one for whom the pressing-stones are yoked, the strainers are moist, the sacrifice is spread out, and the sacrificial rite has been brought forward. 27.
The sacrifice of one who offers [the oblation] is extended to Prajāpati.
He who offers [the oblation] strides after the strides of Prajāpati. 29.

He who [is for] guests is the *āhavanīya* fire; he who is in the house is the *gārhapatya* fire; that in which they cook is the *dakṣiṇāgni*. (30) And indeed, he who eats before his guest eats the merit of both the sacrifice (*iṣṭa*) and the charitable work (*pūrta*) belonging to the household. (31)
He who eats before his guest eats only the milk and the essence of the household.
He who eats before his guest eats indeed the vigor and the prosperity of the household. //33//
He who eats before his guest consumes the offspring, the cattle, and the household of that guest. (AVŚ 9.6.34a)
He who eats before his guest consumes the fame and glory of his household. (AVŚ 9.6.35a)
He who eats before his guest consumes the prosperity and the sacred knowledge of that person's household.
This indeed is the guest: one learned in the Vedas; therefore, one should not eat before him. //37//
When the guest has eaten, one should eat for the sake of the integrity of the sacrifice and the non-interruption of the sacrifice; that is the vow. 38.
(9.6.39a) Indeed, this is even more delicious: whether it be milk from a cow or meat, one should eat that very thing.
{17} (9.6.40a) He who, knowing thus, pours out and offers milk—(9.6.40c) as much as one obtains by performing a well-perfected Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, so much does he obtain by this means. {40}
Whoever, knowing this, offers clarified butter after pouring it out, wins as much as one wins by performing a well-perfected Atirātra sacrifice; so much does he win by this means. //41//
Whoever, knowing thus, offers honey by pouring it out, wins as much as one wins by performing the Sattrasadya sacrifice with great success; that much he wins by this means. //42//
Whoever, knowing thus, sprinkles meat and offers it, wins by this as much as one wins by performing a sacrifice that is perfectly successful for twelve days. //43//
He who, knowing thus, pours out water and offers it, goes for the procreation of offspring; he becomes dear to offspring—he who, knowing thus, pours out water and offers it.
For him, Dawn utters the sound *hiṅ*, and Savitṛ praises him aloud.
Bṛhaspati sings with vigor; Tvaṣṭṛ offers it back with nourishment; the All-gods are the Nidhana. //2//
He who knows thus becomes the culmination of prosperity, progeny, and cattle. //45//
As the sun rises, he utters *hiṃ*; at the time of gathering [the cattle], he chants the *prastāva*;
at midday, he sings the *udgītha*; in the afternoon, he performs the *pratihāra*; and as it sets, he makes the *nidhana*.
He who knows this becomes the *nidhana*—the foundation—of prosperity, progeny, and cattle. 46.
When he becomes a cloud, he utters *hiṃ*; thundering, he performs the *pra-stuti*;
flashing with lightning, he responds; raining, he sings the *ud-gītha*; and ceasing to rain, he performs the *nidhana*.
He who knows this becomes the *nidhana* of prosperity, of progeny, and of cattle. //47//
He looks toward the guests; he makes the sound *hiṅ*; he addresses them; he praises them; he asks for water; he sings the *udgītha*.
He brings food near; he offers it back; the remnants are the *nidhana*.
He who knows this becomes the *nidhana* of prosperity, of offspring, and of cattle. 48. {19}
When he calls the *kṣattṛ*, that is indeed the act of making the announcement. //49//
Whatever one responds to, that indeed is what one causes to be responded to. //50//
Those who approach from the front and from behind, serving as attendants with vessels in their hands, are indeed the *camasādhvaryu* priests.
Among them, there was no one at all who served as the Hotṛ priest. //52//
Or when the master of the house, having served his guests, goes back to his home, he thereby enters the purificatory bath. //53//
When one distributes the sacrificial gifts, one distributes the dakṣiṇās; when one performs the concluding rite, that is indeed the *udavasāna*. //54//
Invited upon the earth, he partakes; invited therein is whatever is of manifold form upon the earth. //55//
Invited, he partakes in the mid-air; invited, he partakes in that which has all forms in heaven. //56//
Invited, he partakes in that which is in heaven; invited, he partakes in whatever is multiform in heaven.
Invited among the gods, he partakes; invited, he partakes in that which is multiform in heaven. 58.
Invoked among the worlds, he partakes; invoked therein is that which is multiform in heaven.
He is invited; he is invited. //60//
He attains this world; he attains that world. //61//
One who knows thus conquers the luminous worlds.
Prajāpati and Parameṣṭhin are the two horns; Indra is the head; Agni is the forehead; Yama is the nape of the neck.
King Soma is the brain; the sky is the upper jaw, and the earth is the lower jaw. //2//
Lightning is his tongue, the Maruts his teeth, Revatī his neck, the Kṛttikās his shoulders, and the Gharma-vessel his carriage. //3//
Vāyu is the all-encompassing, the heavenly world; the black drop is the supporter, to be entered. //4//
The hawk is the ribs; the atmosphere is the breast-bone; Bṛhaspati is the hump; the great [verses] are the vertebrae. //5//
The wives of the gods are the ribs; the Upasad offerings are the sides.
Mitra and Varuṇa are his shoulders; Tvaṣṭṛ and Aryaman are his forearms; Mahādeva is his two arms.
Indrāṇī is the buttocks, Vāyu the tail, and Pavamāna the hair.
The priesthood and the nobility are the hips; strength is the thighs. //9//
Dhātṛ and Savitṛ are the two ankle-bones; the Gandharvas and Apsarases are the shanks; Aditi is the hooves. //10//
The mind, the heart, the liver, the intellect, the sacred vow, and the pericardium. //11//
Hunger is the belly; food is the rectum; the mountains are the entrails. 12.
Anger is the kidneys, resentment is the testicles, and progeny is the penis. //13//
The rivers are its girth-strap; the lord of rain is its udder; the thunder is its teat. //14//
The skin is Viśvavyacas, the herbs are the hair, and the stars are the form. 15.
The divine folk are the intestines; human beings are the entrails; here is the belly. 16.
The *rakṣases* [take] the blood; other people [take] the undigested contents (*ūbadhya*). //17//
The cloud is the swelling marrow; the finale is the foundation.
Agni is seated; the Aśvins are risen. //19//
Indra stands facing the east; Yama stands facing the south.
Dhātṛ stands facing west; Savitṛ stands facing north.
King Soma has reached the grass. //22//
Mitra, looking back, has turned toward bliss. //23//
When being yoked, he belongs to the All-gods; when yoked, he is Prajāpati; when unyoked, he is the All.
This indeed is the omniform, the all-formed, the form of the cow.
(26) Cattle of every form and all forms stand near him who knows thus.
(1) Head-ache, affliction of the head, ear-ache, and blood-red inflammation—
every disease of the head we charm away from you with our spells.
From your ears, from the *kaṅkūṣas*, the ear-ache and the *visalpaka*—all the disease located in your head, we charm away externally. //2//
For whatever reason the consumption (yakṣma) departs from the ear or from the mouth—every disease of the head, we conjure it out from you with this mantra. 3.
He who makes one senseless, he who makes a man blind—
every disease of yours that is in the head, we charm it out with a spell.
The breaking of limbs, fever of the limbs, that which affects all parts of the body, and erysipelas—
every disease of yours located in the head, we charm out to the outside.
Whose terrifying appearance causes a person to tremble—
that *takman* which lasts through all autumns— we exorcise outside.
That which creeps along the thighs and likewise goes to the groins—your consumption (*yakṣma*), we conjure out from within your limbs to the outside. //7//
If from desire, or from lack of desire, it is born from the heart; we drive the swelling from the heart and from the limbs outwards with this mantra. //8//
The jaundice from your limbs, the swelling from within your belly, and the seat of the *yakṣman* disease from within your self—we drive them all out to the outside with our mantra. 9.
Let it become consumption, let it become dropsy, let it become a wasting disease;
I have spoken the poison of all consumptive ailments out from you. Let the *kāhābāha* flow out through the external opening from your belly.
I have spoken out from you the poison of all consumptive diseases. 11.
From your belly, from your lungs, from your navel, and from your heart—from all diseases, I have spoken their poison out from you. 12.
Those flowing waters that break down the boundaries and strike against the head—let them flow out through the opening, non-violent and free from disease. 13.
Those that pierce the heart and spread through the ribs— let them, non-violent and harmless, flow out through the external opening.
Those [worms] that crawl along the sides and nibble at the ribs—let them, non-violent and free from disease, run out through the outer opening. 15.
Those flowing streams that flow crosswise into your channels—
let them run out through the opening, non-violent and free from disease.
Those that creep along the intestines and cause delusion of the entrails—let them, non-violent and free from disease, run out through the external opening. 17.
Those who suck out the marrow and break the joints—let them, non-violent and healthy, run out through the opening outside. 18.
The wasting diseases that madden your limbs and cause them to swell—
I have now spoken the poison out from you, from all such wasting diseases.
Of the creeping eruption, of the abscess, of the rheumatism, and of the scab—of all consumptive diseases, I have spoken the poison out from you. 20.
From your feet, from your knees, from your hips and from your loins;
from your spine, from your neck-veins, and from your head—I have destroyed the disease. 21.
May the rising sun with his rays destroy the disease of your head and quell the fracture of your limbs— that which cleaves the skull-caps of your head and that which pierces your heart.
Of this lovely, gray-haired Hotṛ-priest, the middle brother is Aśna.
The third brother is he whose back is anointed with ghee; here I beheld the Lord of the People, who has seven sons. //1//
Seven harness the one-wheeled chariot; a single horse draws it, having seven names.
The wheel has three naves, is ageless and invincible, upon which all these worlds stand. //2//
Upon this seven-wheeled chariot stand the seven; seven horses draw it.
Seven sisters sing together toward it where the seven names of the cows are deposited.
Who has seen the first-born being, when that which is boneless bears the bony?
Where indeed is the life-force, the breath, and the blood of the earth? Who shall go to the one who knows to ask this? 4.
Let him who truly knows it speak here of this lovely bird’s hidden place;
from its head the cows milk forth milk, and wearing its covering, they have reached the water with their feet. //5//
(9.9.6a) As a simpleton, not understanding with my mind, I ask about these footsteps set down by the gods.
(9.9.6c) Upon the young calf, the sages have stretched out seven threads to be woven.
Unaware here even of those who are aware, I ask the wise seers, being myself unwise:
what indeed is that One which, in the form of the Unborn, has propped apart these six worlds? //7//

The mother shared her portion with the father according to the *ṛta*; for in the beginning, she united with him through the mind. Loathing the essence of the embryo, she was pierced; then those who offered homage approached her with a prayer. //8//
Yoked was the Mother at the pole of the sacrificial gift; the Embryo stood within the enclosures. The Calf lowed as he beheld the Cow of manifold forms in her three unions. //9//
Bearing three mothers and three fathers, the One stands erect; they do not cause him to weary.
Upon the back of yonder heaven, those who know all converse in speech that is unknown to all.
Upon the five-spoked wheel as it revolves, all beings rest.
Its axle, though bearing a heavy burden, does not grow hot; its nave, from of old, is never severed.
They say that the Father has five feet, twelve forms, and dwells in the watery realm in the further half of heaven;
while others say he is fixed upon another, lower, far-seeing wheel of seven spokes and six rims.
This wheel of the Cosmic Order, with its twelve spokes, rolls around the sky without aging.
Here, O Agni, stand the sons in pairs—seven hundred and twenty.
The wheel with its rim has turned, undecaying; ten yoked ones carry it upon that which lies extended.
The eye of Sūrya moves through the mid-air, encompassing that in which all beings have taken their stand.
(9.9.15a) Those who are women, they call men to me; he who has eyes sees, yet the blind man does not perceive.
(9.9.15c) The son who is a seer has understood this; he who discerns them shall be the father of his father. //15//
Of those born together, they say the seventh was born alone; these six are the twin seers, born of the gods.
Their desired abodes, established according to their stations, tremble for the Creator, manifested in various forms.
Beneath the higher realm and above this lower one, the cow has risen up, bearing her calf with her foot.
Whither has she gone? To which side has she departed? Where indeed will she give birth, for she is not in this herd?
Who knows this father who is below the lower region, or him who is above the upper region and beyond the lower?
Acting as a seer, who here can declare from where the divine mind was born? 18.
Those which they call "hitherward," they call "thitherward"; those which they call "thitherward," they call "hitherward.
O Indra and Soma, those things which you two have fashioned are carried like yoked horses through the mid-air.
Two birds, united and companions, cling to the same tree.
Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating.
On whatever tree all the fair-winged ones who eat honey settle and breed, that which they call its sweet fruit at the top—may that never reach him who does not know his father. 21.
(9.9.22a) Where the fair-winged ones, without blinking, cry out together toward the draught of immortality;
(9.9.22c) there the wise guardian of this entire world has entered into me, the simple one.
{25} (9.10.1a) When the Gāyatra is placed upon the Gāyatra, or when they have fashioned the Triṣṭubh from the Triṣṭubh—
Or whatever moving thing has been placed within the Jagatī meter—those who know that have attained immortality. //1//

With the *gāyatrī* he measures out the *arká*; with the *arká*, the *sāman*; with the *triṣṭubh*, the *vāk*. With the *vāk* they measure out the *vāk*: the two-footed and the four-footed; by means of the syllable, they measure out the seven voices. //2//
With the Jagatī he propped up the Sindhu in heaven; in the Rathantara he beheld the sun.
They say there are three kindling-sticks of the Gāyatra; from there it has surpassed [all] by its greatness and majesty. //3//
I invoke this well-milking cow; may the milker with skillful hands milk her.
May Savitṛ impel for us the most excellent impulse. The *gharma* has been heated; let him proclaim that very thing. 4.
Making the sound *hiṅ*, the mistress of treasures has come hither, seeking her calf with her mind.
May this inviolable cow yield milk for the two Aśvins; may she increase for our great good fortune. //5//
The cow has lowed toward the blinking calf; she has made the "hiṅ" sound upon his head to measure him out.
Lowing toward the warm milk, she utters her cry; she yields her milk with her streams of milk.
This is that which bellows, by which the cow is encompassed; she lowing like a wild beast rests upon the cleft of the mountain.
By her thoughts she has indeed surpassed mortals; becoming lightning, she cast off her covering.
The life-breath, moving and unaging, dwells within the firm and trembling waters in the midst of the dwellings.
Living by means of the funeral offerings of the dead, the immortal shares a common womb with the mortal.
The gray-haired one has swallowed the young moon as it hastens upon the back of the waters.
Behold the poetic power of the god; through his greatness, he who was alive today has died yesterday. 9.
(9.10.10) He who made this does not know it; he who saw it is indeed far removed from it.
Enveloped within his mother’s womb, Nirṛti, though possessing many offspring, has entered therein.
(9.10.11) I beheld the Herdsman, who never rests, moving hither and thither along his paths.
Clothed in converging and diverging rays, he revolves repeatedly within the worlds. //11//
Heaven is our father, our progenitor; here is our navel. This great earth is our kin, our mother.
Between the two upturned bowls is the womb; therein the father placed the seed of his daughter. 12.
I ask you about the furthest limit of the earth; I ask about the seed of the stallion.
I ask about the navel of the entire world; I ask about the highest heaven of speech. 13.
This altar is the furthest limit of the earth; this Soma is the seed of the potent horse.
This sacrifice is the navel of the entire world; this Brahman is the supreme vault of speech. 14.
I do not discern what this is that I am; hidden and armored, I move with my mind.
When the first-born of Cosmic Order comes to me, then indeed I obtain a share of this Speech. //15//
Westward and eastward he goes, held by his own inherent power; the immortal is of common origin with the mortal.
These two, eternal and moving in opposite directions, pass away; men perceive one, but they do not perceive the other.

Seven half-germs, the seed of the world, abide by the command of Viṣṇu in the established order; through their insights and their mind, they, the wise ones, as encompassers, encompass all things on every side. //17//
In the syllable of the *ṛc*, in the highest heaven, upon which all the gods have settled—what will he do with the *ṛc* who does not know that? But those who know it, they sit together there. //18//
Fashioning the foot of the *ṛc* with its measure, they formed all that moves by means of the half-verse.
The three-footed Brahman, assuming many forms, has spread itself out; by it the four quarters of space live. //19//
May you indeed be blessed with good pasture; may we likewise be blessed.
Eat grass, O inviolable one, at all times; drink pure water as you wander.
The Cow has lowed, fashioning the waters; she is one-footed, two-footed, and four-footed.
Having become eight-footed, nine-footed, and thousand-syllabled, she is the fivefold array of the world; from her the oceans flow forth.
The black path, the tawny-winged birds, clothed in the waters, fly up to heaven.
They have turned back from the seat of Cosmic Order; indeed, they have overspread the earth with clarified butter.
The footless one goes forth, the first among those that have feet; who, O Mitra and Varuṇa, has understood this of yours?
The embryo bears the burden of this very [cow]; he fulfills the *ṛta* and guards against the *anṛta*. 23.
Virāj is speech; Virāj is the earth; Virāj is the intermediate space; Virāj is Prajāpati;
Virāj became Mṛtyu, the sovereign ruler of the Sādhyas. Under his control are the past and the future; may he bring the past and the future under my control. //24//
I saw from afar, beyond the nearer [world], the smoke made of *śaka*-wood spreading in every direction.
The heroes cooked the dappled bull; those were the first ordinances. //25//
Three long-haired ones appear in due season; one of them shears [the hair] within the year. Another beholds the universe with his powers; the speed of the third is seen, but not his form.
Speech has been measured out in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them.
Three, hidden in secret, do not stir; of speech, mortals speak only the fourth quarter. //27//
They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni; and he is the divine, fair-winged Garuḍa.
That which is one, the sages speak of as manifold; they call it Agni, Yama, and Mātariśvan.
The physicians fashion her, like a bride for the wedding procession, multiform and fashioned by their hands.
Having reached its core, let us drive her away. //1//
Headed, possessed of a nose, possessed of ears, fashioned by a sorcerer, assembled, and multiform—let her depart from here;
we drive her away.
Whether committed by a Śūdra, by a king, by a woman, or by Brahmins—like a wife driven away by her husband, let it seize the doer as its kinsman. //3//
By means of this herb, I have corrupted all sorceries—
those which they have wrought upon the field, those upon the cattle, or those upon your men.
Let there be evil for the evildoer; let the curse recoil upon him who utters it. We send it back against him, so that it may destroy the one who fashioned the sorcery.
Facing westward is the descendant of Aṅgiras, our overseer and domestic priest; turning back the sorceries, strike down those who practice sorcery against us.
(7) That which said to you, "Go away," speaking contrary to what is right— turn back upon that *kṛtyā*, and do not seek us, who are innocent.
He who joined together your limbs with wisdom, like a craftsman [reconstructs] a chariot—go to him; there is your path thither; these people here are unknown to you. //8//
Those wise sorcerers who, having prepared you, have seized you—by means of this *śambhu* [remedy] which destroys magic spells, the counter-path, and the *punaḥsara*, we bathe you with it. 9.
Whatever ill fortune we have encountered— whether from one who has been bathed for purification, or from one whose offspring has died— let all that evil depart from me, and let wealth abide with me.
Whatever name they have taken for you while giving to the ancestors or at the sacrifice, [may it be auspicious].
May these plants release you from every harmful thing that has been sent against you. //11//
From the sin against the gods, from that against the ancestors, from the curse uttered by name, and from the pointed accusation—
may the plants release you by their power, by the sacred word, by the *ṛg* verses, and by the milk of the seers.
Just as the wind shakes the dust from the earth and the cloud from the atmosphere, even so, O Brahman, may all that is ill-fated be driven away from me. 13.
Depart, you howling one, bound like a she-ass;
go to the makers from here, driven away by powerful sacred word (*brahman*).
"This is the path; we lead you here, thinking 'it must be done. We send you forth against the one who has been sent against us.
Go forth with that [path], like a wagon-drawing team that breaks through, multiform and all-accomplishing."
Far away is your light; turn your path back toward us; make your course elsewhere than with us.
Go beyond the ninety navigable rivers and across the difficult streams; do not linger, go forth!
Like the wind crushing the trees, strike them down; leave not a cow, a horse, nor a man remaining among them. Turn back the doers from here; awaken this ritual act (*kṛtyā*) for their childlessness.
The sorcery or the hidden spell that they buried for you upon the sacrificial grass, in the cemetery, or in the field;
or that they practiced against you at the Gārhapatya fire—those more cunning ones, though you were innocent and simple-minded.
The enmity that was brought forward, recognized, buried, and driven deep—we have found the perpetrator.
Let it go back to where it was brought from; let it turn back like a horse, and let it destroy the offspring of the sorcerers.

Well-forged swords are in our house; we know your limbs, O *kṛtyā*, in all their parts. Arise, go away from here! O unknown one, what do you seek here? (20) I shall cut off your necks and your feet, O *kṛtyā*; run away! (21)
May Indra and Agni protect us, they who are the progenitors of offspring for all creatures. 21.
May King Soma, the sovereign, and the compassionate lords of all beings show us mercy. //22//
May Bhava and Śarva hurl the lightning, the weapon of the gods, at the evildoer, the performer of sorcery, and the doer of evil. 23.
Whether you have come as a two-footed or a four-footed creature, fashioned by magic, assembled, and possessing every form—
becoming eight-footed, O bringer of misfortune, go back again!
Anointed, well-adorned, and beautifully decorated, carrying away all misfortune, depart!
Know, O Kṛtyā, your maker as a daughter knows her own father. 25.
Go away, O Kṛtyā; do not stay! Lead her away like the track of a wounded animal.
She is a deer and you are a hunter; you ought not to harm her.
Moreover, one archer, taking up his bow, strikes down another who is already seated;
furthermore, while the first is striking, the other strikes him back. 27.
Listen indeed to these words of mine: go back to the place from which you came; return to him who made you. 28.
The slaying of the innocent is indeed terrible; O witchcraft, do not kill our cow, horse, or man.
Wherever you have been laid down, from there we raise you up: become lighter than a leaf.
If you are shrouded in darkness, as if caught in a net— O all you *kṛtyās*, we tear you apart and send you back to your maker.
The performer of spells, the one who buries charms, the one who brings them forth—crush their offspring!
O spell, do not leave any behind; slay those performers of spells! 31.

Just as the sun is released from darkness, leaving behind the night and the signs of dawn, even so do I leave behind all that is ill-fated, every deed wrought by a sorcerer or a practitioner of magic; like an elephant shaking off dust, I cast off misfortune.
By whom were the heels of man brought together? By whom was the flesh gathered? By whom were the ankles formed?
By whom were the fingers fashioned? By whom the apertures? By whom the two shoulders from the middle? And by whom the foundation? //1//
Why indeed did they make the ankles below and the kneecaps above for the man? Having fashioned the shanks, where did they place them? Where are the joints of the knees; who has understood that? 2.
They join the four [limbs] ending at the joints; the trunk is loose above the knees.
Who indeed produced the hips and the thighs, by which the well-firm *kusindha* came into being? //3//

How many were the gods, and who were they, who fashioned the chest and the neck of Puruṣa? How many assigned the two breasts, who [assigned] the two shoulders, how many built the shoulder-blades, and how many the ribs? //4//
Who brought together his two arms, saying, "Let him perform heroic deeds"? Which god placed those shoulders upon his back for him? //5//
Who pierced the seven openings in the head— these two ears, the two nostrils, the two eyes, and the mouth—
through which the four-footed and two-footed creatures go their way according to the greatness of victory in many places?
For he placed the far-reaching tongue within the jaws; then he set the great voice upon it.
He moves repeatedly within the worlds, clothing himself in the waters—who indeed has understood that? 7.
Which god, having first piled his brain, his forehead, his temple, and his skull, and having built up the two jaws of the man as a structure to be piled, ascended to heaven? Who is that god? //8//
Why does a man carry many things pleasant and unpleasant, dreams, oppression, and weariness, as well as joys and delights, O Mighty One? (AVŚ 10.2.9)

Whence come affliction, distress, destruction, and the lack of understanding in man? Whence come success, prosperity, failure, intelligence, and the dawns? (10) Who placed within this [man] the waters that flow in all directions, flowing in many ways, born for the rushing of rivers? (11)
Intense, ruddy, red, coppery-smoky—upward, downward, and across within the person. //11//
Who placed form in him? Who [placed] greatness and name?
Who [placed] the path in him? Who the signal? Who the various movements in the person? 12.
Who wove the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the in-breath (*apāna*), and the diffused breath (*vyāna*) into this [person]?
Which god established the common breath (*samāna*) within this person? 13.
(10.2.14a) Which one god placed the sacrifice within this person?
(10.2.14c) Who [placed] truth in him, who falsehood? Whence death, whence immortality? //14//
Who put the garment upon him? Who ordained his life-span?
Who bestowed strength upon him? Who provided him with speed? (15)
By whom was the water stretched out? By whom did he create the day for the sake of light? By whom did he kindle the dawn? By whom was the evening state bestowed? (16)
Who placed the seed within this [embryo], thinking, "Let the thread be stretched out"? Who infused wisdom into it? Who placed the arrow, who the dancer? //17//
By what did he cover this earth? By what did he encompass the sky? By what greatness does he pervade the mountains? By what [does] the Puruṣa [pervade] his deeds? (18)
By what does one follow Parjanya? By what, the far-seeing Soma?
By what, both sacrifice and faith? By what is the mind placed within this [body]? 19.
(20) By what does one attain the *śrotriya*, and by what this *parameṣṭhin*? By what does a person attain this *agni*, and by what does he measure the year?
(21) Through *brahman* one attains the *śrotriya*; through *brahman* this *parameṣṭhin*.
The Puruṣa has measured this Brahman-Agni as the year-long Brahman. //21//
By what does one dwell among the gods? By what, among the clans of divine origin?
By what is this other constellation [defined], and by what is true sovereignty (*kṣatra*) called such? //22//
The sacred word dwells among the gods; the sacred word dwells among the divine clans.
This other constellation is the sacred word; the sacred word is called true sovereignty.
By whom was this earth fashioned? By whom was the sky placed above? By whom was this wide intermediate space established, both upwards and across? 24.
By the Brahman the earth was established; by the Brahman the higher heaven was placed above.
By the Brahman this expanse of the intermediate space, both upwards and across, was established. 25.
Having sewn together his head and his heart, Atharvan sent him forth from the brain, upward from the head, as he was being purified.
That indeed is the head of Atharvan, the divine casket closed up;
that the vital breath protects—the head, the food, and also the mind.
Was he created upright? Was he created horizontal? The Puruṣa has pervaded all the quarters.
He who knows that city of Brahman, of which the Puruṣa is said to be the name. //28//
To him who indeed knows that city of Brahman, which is enveloped by immortality—to him Brahman and the Brahmans have granted sight, breath, and progeny. //29//
Neither the eye nor the breath abandons him before old age,
who knows the city of Brahman, of which the Puruṣa is said to be the name.
The city of the gods, with eight wheels and nine gates, is unassailable; within it is a golden treasury, the heavenly realm enveloped in light.
In that golden casket, three-spoked and triple-supported,
whatever self-possessed spirit resides therein, that indeed the knowers of Brahman perceive.
Radiant, golden-hued, and completely surrounded by glory,
the Brahman has entered the unconquerable golden city.
This amulet of mine, made of *varaṇa* wood, is a bull that destroys rivals.
With that, seize the enemies; crush those who seek to do you harm. //1//
Crush the enemies! Crush them! Seize them! Let this amulet be your forerunner in front.
With the *varaṇa* plant, the gods warded off the assault of the Asuras day after day. 2.
This amulet is a warder-off, possessing all healing powers; it is thousand-eyed, greenish-yellow, and golden.
May it cast your enemies down beneath you; first, destroy those who hate you. //3//
This *varaṇa* tree shall ward you off from the spell spread against you, from this human fear, and from every evil.
May this divine tree, Varaṇa, ward it off;
may the gods drive away the consumption that has entered into him.
If, having fallen asleep, you see an evil dream— such as a deer running along an undesirable path—
this Varana amulet shall ward off the ill-omened sneeze and the evil speech of the bird.
From ill-will, from destruction, from malevolent magic, and likewise from fear— from the deadly blow of death more powerful than the powerful— the *varaṇa* tree shall ward you off.
Whatever sin my mother, my father, my brothers, or my own kin have committed, and whatever we ourselves have done—may this divine Lord of the Forest ward it off from us. (AVŚ 10.3.8)
My rivals, together with their kinsmen, have been utterly shaken by the *varaṇa* plant;
they have entered the unfrequented dust, let them go down into the lowest darkness. 9.
Unharmed am I, with an unharmed teacher, long-lived and full of men.
May this Varuṇa amulet protect me from every direction.
This Varuṇa upon my breast is a king, a divine lord of the forest.
May he drive away my enemies, as Indra drove away the Dasyus and the Asuras.
I carry this *varaṇa* tree, may I be long-lived for a hundred autumns;
may it bestow upon me sovereignty, dominion, cattle, and vital strength.
Just as the wind breaks down the lords of the forest, the trees, with its might, so do you shatter my rivals—those born before as well as those born after. May the *varaṇa* tree protect you. 13.
Just as the wind and fire consume the trees and the lords of the forest, so do thou consume my rivals—those born before as well as those born after. May Varaṇa protect thee. 14.
Just as trees, utterly wasted by the wind, lie prostrate, even so do you waste my rivals and cast them down.
May the *varaṇa* tree protect you from those born before as well as those born after. 15.
Cut them down, O Varaṇa, before their appointed time, before the end of their life—
those who seek to harm him regarding his cattle, and those who seek to harm his kingdom.
Just as the sun shines intensely, just as splendor is deposited within it, so may the Varuṇa amulet bestow upon me fame and prosperity.
May it sprinkle me with brilliance; may it anoint me with glory. 17.
Just as glory resides in the moon and in the sun that beholds men, so may the Varuṇa amulet bestow upon me fame and prosperity. May it sprinkle me with splendor; may it anoint me with glory. 18.
As glory is upon the earth, as it is in this Jātavedas, so may the Varuṇa amulet bestow upon me renown and prosperity.
May it sprinkle me with splendor; may it anoint me with glory. 19.

As there is glory in a maiden, as there is [glory] in this well-equipped chariot, even so may the Varaṇa amulet bestow upon me fame and prosperity. May it sprinkle me with splendor; may it anoint me with glory. 20. {8}
As there is glory in the drinking of Soma, as there is glory in the honey-mixture, even so may the Varuṇa amulet bestow upon me fame and prosperity.
May it sprinkle me with splendor; may it anoint me with glory. 21.
As glory resides in the Agnihotra and as glory resides in the Vaṣaṭ-call, even so may the Varuṇa amulet bestow upon me fame and prosperity.
May it sprinkle me with splendor and anoint me with glory. 22.
Just as glory is in the sacrificer, just as it is bestowed upon this sacrifice, so may the Varuṇa amulet bestow upon me fame and prosperity.
May it sprinkle me with splendor; may it anoint me with glory. 23.
Just as glory resides in Prajāpati, and just as it resides in this Parameṣṭhin, so may the Varuṇa amulet bestow upon me fame and prosperity.
May it sprinkle me with splendor; may it anoint me with glory. 24.

Just as immortality is among the gods, and just as truth is established within them, so may the Varana amulet bestow upon me fame and prosperity. May it sprinkle me with splendor; may it anoint me with glory. 25. {9}
Indra’s is the first chariot; the gods’ is the second chariot; Varuṇa’s is the third.
The lowest chariot of the serpents has struck the pillar and then sped away. 1.
The *darbha* grass, the flame, the young sprout, the tail-hair of the horse, the tail-hair of the wild ass, and the seat of the chariot. //2//
Strike it down, O White One, with your foot—both from the front and from behind—like a piece of wood floating on water; render the serpents' poison sapless, as fierce as a torrential flood.
Having submerged and emerged again, Araṅghuṣa spoke:
"Like a piece of wood floating upon the water, the poison of the snakes is sapless; their fierce venom is but water."
The *paidva* slays the *kasarṇīla*, the *paidva* [slays] the white and the black;
the *paidva* has shattered the head of the *ratharvī* and the *pṛdākvā*. //5//
O horse of Pedu, go forth as the first; we follow after you.
Drive the serpents away from the path by which we come.
Here the dog was born; here is its place of departure.
These are the tracks of the horse, the slayer of snakes, the possessor of prize-winning strength.
The closed [jaws] shall not open, nor shall the opened close.
In this field there are two snakes, a female and a male; both of them are sapless.
Tasteless here are the serpents, those that are near and those that are far away;
with a club I strike the scorpion, and with a staff the serpent that has approached.
This is the remedy for Aghāśva and for both kinds of Svaja.
Indra has delivered to me the serpent who was seeking to harm; the serpent-slayer Paidva has subdued him. We meditate upon Paidva, the steadfast one whose foundation is firm.
These vipers sit watching intently from behind.
Their life-breaths destroyed, their poison destroyed, they have been slain by Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt;
Indra has struck them down, and we have struck them down.
Slain are the cross-striped snakes; crushed are the vipers. Strike down the black, white-spotted creature that has made itself a ladle upon the *darbha* grass.
The maiden Kairātikā digs for the medicine with golden spades upon the ridges of the mountains.
This young physician has come, the unvanquished destroyer of *pṛśni*.
He is indeed the crusher of the *svaja* and of both kinds of scorpion. 15.
Indra has subdued the serpent for me, as have Mitra and Varuṇa, and both Vāta and Parjanya. //16//
Indra has delivered for me the *ahi*, the *pṛdāku*, and the *pṛdākva*;
the *svaja* with its transverse stripes, the *kasarṇīla*, and the *daśonaśi*.
Indra struck down your first progenitor, O Ahi.
Of those being crushed, what indeed was their essence?
For I have seized their heads, as a fisherman seizes a large fish;
having gone to the middle of the river, I have washed away the poison of the serpent.
May the rivers carry away the poison of all the snakes. Slain are the *tiraścirājayaḥ*; crushed are the *pṛdākavaḥ*.
From among the plants, I choose [the best] as one chooses fertile fields with skill.
I lead you away like mares; let the poison go out! 21.
Whatever poison is in the fire, in the sun, on the earth, or in the plants—whatever *kāndāviṣa* and *kanaknaka* there may be—let that poison go out; let your poison depart! 22.

Those born from fire, those born from plants, those of the serpents who were born from the waters as lightning—those whose offspring are great in many ways, to those serpents we pay homage with reverence. 23.
You are the maiden named Taudī, or you are indeed named Ghṛtācī.
With my foot, I step upon your footprint, which neutralizes poison. 24.
Make it fall from limb after limb; avoid the heart.
Then let whatever fiery power belongs to your poison go downward into you. 25.
Poison has gone far away; poison has roared against poison; even before it reached [its mark], poison has been repelled.
Agni has cast the poison out from the serpent; Soma has led it away.
The poison has followed after the fang; the serpent has become immortal. 26. {12}
(1) You are the vigor of Indra; you are the force of Indra; you are the strength of Indra; you are the heroism of Indra; you are the manly power of Indra.
For the victorious yoking, I yoke you with the yokes of prayer. 1.
(10.5.2a) You are the vigor of Indra; you are the power of Indra; you are the strength of Indra; you are the heroism of Indra; you are the manliness of Indra.
(10.5.2c) For the victorious yoking, I yoke you with the yokes of sovereignty. //2//
You are the vigor of Indra; you are the power of Indra; you are the strength of Indra; you are the heroism of Indra; you are the manliness of Indra.
For the victorious yoking, I yoke you with the yokes of Indra.
(4a) You are the vigor of Indra; you are the power of Indra; you are the strength of Indra; you are the heroism of Indra; you are the manliness of Indra.
(4c) For victorious application, I yoke you with Soma-applications.
You are the vigor of Indra; you are the force of Indra; you are the strength of Indra; you are the heroism of Indra; you are the manly power of Indra.
For the victorious application, I join you with the applications of water.
(6a) You are the vigor of Indra; you are the power of Indra; you are the strength of Indra; you are the heroism of Indra; you are the manliness of Indra.
(6c) For the victorious harnessing, may all beings wait upon me; harnessed for me, you are the waters.
You are the portion of Agni; the brilliance of the waters. O divine waters, bestow splendor upon us.
By the ordinance of Prajāpati, I settle you for this world.
(10.5.8a) You are the portion of Indra; you are the brilliance of the waters. O divine waters, bestow splendor upon us!
(10.5.8c) By the ordinance of Prajāpati, I settle you for this world. //8//
You are the portion of Soma; you are the brilliance of the waters. O divine waters, bestow splendor upon us.
By the ordinance of Prajāpati, I settle you for this world. 9.
(10a) You are the portion of Varuṇa; O divine waters, bestow upon us the brilliance of the waters, the pure essence.
(10c) By the ordinance of Prajāpati, I set you down for this world.
//10// (11a) You are the portion of Mitra and Varuṇa; O divine waters, bestow upon us the brilliance of the waters, the pure essence.
By the ordinance of Prajāpati, I set you down for this world. //11//
You are the portion of Yama; O divine waters, bestow upon us the brightness of the waters and splendor.
By the ordinance of Prajāpati, I set you down for this world. 12.
You are the portion of the ancestors; O divine waters, bestow brilliance upon us from the essence of the waters.
By the ordinance of Prajāpati, I set you down for this world. 13.
You are the portion of the god Savitṛ; O divine waters, bestow upon us the brilliance of the waters.
By the ordinance of Prajāpati, I set you down for this world. 14.
Whatever portion of the waters is yours, within the waters, fit for sacrifice and a place for the worship of the gods—this I release upon him. Do not cast it back upon me.
With that we release it against him who hates us and whom we hate.
May I strike him down, may I lay him low with this sacred prayer, with this ritual act, and with this curse. 15.
O Waters, that wave of yours which is within the waters, worthy of sacrifice and the place for worshiping the gods—this one I cast away from here; do not let it overwhelm me.
With it, we cast away him who hates us and whom we hate.
I would strike him down, I would lay him low, by this sacred prayer (*brahman*), by this rite (*karman*), and by this curse (*menī*). 16.
O Waters, he who is the calf of the waters, within the waters, worthy of sacrifice, the place of divine worship—him I release here; do not cast him back into me.
By means of him, we release that one who hates us and whom we hate.
I would slay him, I would strike him down with this sacred formula, with this rite, and with this curse. 17.
He who is the bull of the waters, within the waters, worthy of sacrifice, the one to whom the gods offer worship.
I release this against him; do not let it fall upon me. With it, we release it against him who hates us and whom we hate.
May I strike him down, may I lay him low by this sacred prayer, by this ritual act, and by this curse. 18.
O Waters, he who is the golden germ (*hiraṇyagarbha*) within the waters, worthy of sacrifice and the place of divine worship—him I cast away from here; do not let him sink down upon me.
With him we cast away him who hates us and whom we hate.
May I strike him down, may I lay him low by this sacred prayer, by this ritual act, and by this curse. 19.
The stone of the waters, speckled and divine, which dwells within the waters, worthy of sacrifice and the place of worship for the gods—this one I release; do not cast it back upon me.
By means of it, we release him who hates us and whom we hate.
May I strike him down, may I lay him low by this sacred prayer, by this rite, and by this curse. 20.

O Waters, that fire of yours which is within the waters, worthy of sacrifice and the place of divine worship—this one I release; do not cast it back upon me. With it we release him who hates us and whom we hate.
May I strike him down, may I lay him low by this sacred word (*brahman*), by this ritual act (*karman*), and by this spell (*menī*). 21.
Whatever falsehood we have uttered within the last three years—may the waters protect me from all that evil and from distress. 22.
I send you forth to the ocean; go back to your own source. Unharmed, with all your vigor intact, may nothing whatsoever cause us pain.
The waters are free from blemish; may they carry away the blemish from us.
May those of beautiful countenance carry away from us sin, misfortune, evil dreams, and impurity. 24.
(10.5.25a) You are Viṣṇu’s stride, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by the earth, with the brilliance of Agni.
(10.5.25c) Following the earth, I stride forth; from the earth we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
(10.5.25e) May he not live; may the vital breath abandon him! 25.

(10.5.26a) You are Viṣṇu’s stride, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by the intermediate region, with the brilliance of Vāyu. (10.5.26c) I stride across the intermediate region. From the intermediate region we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
(10.5.26e) May he not live; may breath abandon him! 26.
You are the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by heaven, with the brilliance of the sun. Following heaven, I stride forth. From heaven we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
May he not live; may breath abandon him! 27.
(10.5.28a) You are the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by the quarters, with mind as your brilliance.
(10.5.28c) Following the quarters, I stride forth; from the quarters we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
(10.5.28e) May he not live; may breath desert him! 28.

(29a) You are the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by hope, with the brilliance of the wind. (29c) I stride across the quarters; from the quarters we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
(29e) May he not live; may breath abandon him! 29.

Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by the Ṛgveda and possessing the splendor of the Sāmaveda. Following the Ṛgverses, I stride forth; from the Ṛgverses we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
May he not live; may breath abandon him! 30. {15}
(10.5.31a) You are Viṣṇu’s stride, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by sacrifice, possessing the splendor of Brahman.
(10.5.31c) Following the sacrifice, I step forth; from the sacrifice we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
(10.5.31e) May he not live; may the vital breath abandon him! //31//

You are the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by the plants, possessing the splendor of Soma. Following the plants, I step forth; from the plants we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
May he not live; may the vital breath abandon him! 32.

Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of rivals, sharpened in the waters, possessing the splendor of Varuṇa. Following the waters, I step forth; from the waters we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
May he not live; may breath abandon him! 33.
(10.5.34a) You are the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by agriculture, possessing the luster of food.
(10.5.34c) Following after agriculture, I stride forth; through agriculture we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
(10.5.34e) May he not live; may the breath of life abandon him! //34//
Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by breath, possessing the brilliance of man.
Following after breath, I stride forth; from breath we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
May he not live; may breath abandon him! 35.
Victory is ours; we have prevailed. I have overcome all hostile armies.
Here I encircle the luster, the brilliance, the breath, and the life-force of the son of such-and-such a lineage and such-and-such a mother. Here I cast him down beneath my feet. 36.
I turn following the turning of the sun, following the turning of the south.
May she grant me wealth; may she grant me the splendor of sacred knowledge.
I turn toward the luminous quarters;
may they grant me wealth, and may they grant me the splendor of sacred knowledge.
I turn toward the Seven Seers;
may they grant me wealth, may they grant me the luster of sacred knowledge.
I turn toward the Brahman; may they grant me that wealth, may they grant me that splendor of the Brahmin.
(40) I turn toward the Brahmins.
May they grant me wealth; may they grant me the splendor of Brahmanical luster. //41//
Whomever we seek, him we strike down with weapons; within the gaping mouth of Parameṣṭhin, we have cast him by means of the sacred word (*brahman*). 42.
With the two tusks of Vaiśvānara, let the weapon strike him down;
may this oblation, the divine and most powerful kindling-stick, devour him. 43.
You are the bond of King Varuṇa.
Bind such-and-such a man, the son of such-and-such a man and such-and-such a woman, to food and to breath. 44.
O Lord of the Earth, that food of yours which overflows across the earth—grant us a share of that, O Lord of the Earth, O Prajāpati. (45)
I have sought the divine waters; we have been united with their essence.
Rich in milk, O Agni, I have come; endow me with splendor. //46//
O Agni, unite me with splendor, unite me with progeny, and unite me with long life.
May the gods take note of this of mine; may Indra, together with the seers, take note.
O Agni, whatever curse the pair utters today, or whatever harsh speech the singers produce—whatever arrow is born from the wrath of the mind—with that pierce the sorcerers in their hearts. 48.
Crush the sorcerers with your heat; O Agni, crush the *rakṣas* with your flame.
Crush the worshippers of foolish gods with your radiance; crush those who feast on life-breath as they burn away. 49.
I, the wise one, hurl the four-edged thunderbolt of the waters at him for the splitting of his head. May it shatter all his limbs; may all the gods acknowledge this deed of mine.
The head of the enemy, the rival, the ill-hearted hater—[I strike it down].
I even cut it away by my power. //1//
This amulet, born from the plowshare, shall provide me with armor;
may it come to me full with its stirring-stick, together with sap and splendor.
If a skillful carpenter has struck you with his hand and axe,
may the pure, life-giving waters purify you, the pure one, from that.
This jewel, adorned with a golden garland, bestowing faith, sacrifice, and greatness—may it dwell as a guest in our house. 4.
For him we offer ghee, wine, honey, and food upon food.
May he, like a father for his sons, provide for us what is better and better; may the amulet, coming day after day from the gods, bring us prosperity more and more.

The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound on—a plow that drips with ghee, fierce, and full of vigor—Agni fastened it upon himself; it yielded for him clarified butter more and more, day after day. With that, do thou slay thy enemies.
The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound on—a plowshare dripping with ghee, fierce, and a weapon for vigor—Indra fastened it upon himself for vigor and for manly power.
It yields him strength indeed, more and more, day after day; with that, do thou slay thy enemies. 7.
The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound on—the plowshare dripping with ghee, the fierce *kadhira* for the sake of vigor—that Soma fastened upon him for great hearing and sight.
It yields him luster more and more, day after day; with that, do thou slay thy enemies. 8.
The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound on—a ploughshare dripping with ghee, fierce, made of khadira wood for the sake of vigor—Sūrya fastened upon himself; with it he conquered these quarters.
It yields prosperity to him more and more, day after day; with that, do you slay your enemies. 9.

The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound on—the plowshare dripping with ghee, the fierce one made of khadira wood for the sake of vigor—wearing that moon-like amulet, he conquered the golden fortresses of the Asuras, the Dānavas.
It yields him prosperity more and more, day after day; with it, do you slay your enemies. 10. {18}
The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the swift wind—may it yield him vigorous strength more and more, day after day; with that, do thou slay thy enemies. 11.
The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the swift wind—by means of that amulet, O Aśvins, you two protect this cultivation.
Through those two physicians, it yields great abundance day after day, more and more; with it, do thou slay thy enemies. 12.

The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the swift wind—wearing that amulet, Savitṛ won this heaven with it. It milks out abundance for him, more and more, day after day; with it, do you slay your enemies. 13.

The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the swift wind—carrying that amulet, the inexhaustible waters always flow. It yields nectar to them more and more, day after day; with that, do you slay your enemies. 14.
The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the swift wind—King Varuṇa fastened that auspicious amulet upon himself. It yields him truth more and more, day after day; with it, do thou slay thy enemies. 15.
The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the swift wind—carrying that amulet, the gods conquered all the worlds in battle.
It yields them victory more and more, day after day; with it, do you slay your enemies. 16.
The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the swift wind—this auspicious amulet the deities fastened on again.
It milks everything from these [beings] more and more, day after day; with it, do thou slay thy enemies. 17.
The seasons bound him; the seasonal periods bound him.
Having bound him, the year guards all that has come to be.
The intermediate regions bound him; the cardinal directions bound him.
This amulet, created by Prajāpati, has cast my enemies beneath me. 19.
The Atharvans bound it; the descendants of Atharvan bound it.
With those [bonds], the Aṅgirases, acting as allies, shattered the fortresses of the Dasyus; with that, do you slay your enemies.
(20) The Creator fastened it on; he fashioned the world of beings.
With that, do you slay your enemies. //21//
That amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the gods as a protection against the Asuras—
may it come to me with sap and with luster.
That amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the gods as a protection against the Asuras—that amulet has come to me, together with cattle, goats, sheep, food, and progeny. 23.
That amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the gods as a protection against the Asuras—that amulet has come to me, together with rice and barley, along with glory and prosperity. 24.
That which Bṛhaspati bound for the gods as a protection against the Asuras—may that amulet come to me with a stream of honey and ghee, together with the *kīlāla* juice. 25.
That amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the gods, providing protection against the Asuras—may that amulet come to me, together with vigor, with milk, with wealth, and with glory. 26.
That which Bṛhaspati bound for the gods as a protection against the Asuras—that amulet has come to me, together with splendor and brilliance, together with glory and fame. 27.
That which Bṛhaspati bound for the gods as a protection against the Asuras—that amulet has come to me together with all prosperities. 28.
May the deities grant me this amulet for prosperity—this amulet that is all-conquering, that increases dominion, and that subdues rivals. 29.
With sacred power (*brahman*) and splendor (*tejas*), I fasten upon myself what is auspicious for me.
Without rivals, a slayer of rivals, he has cast my rivals beneath me.
(30) May this jewel, born of the gods, make me superior to my enemies.
He whose milk these three worlds drink as their nourishment—
may that amulet ascend upon my head for preeminence.
That upon which gods, ancestors, and humans always depend for their livelihood—
may that amulet ascend to my head for preeminence.
Just as a seed sown in a ploughed field grows, so may offspring, cattle, and food upon food grow within me. 33.
O amulet, increaser of the sacrifice, for whomsoever I have fastened you on as a blessing—
do you, O amulet of a hundredfold dakṣiṇā, quicken him to preeminence.
O Agni, graciously accepting this well-prepared fuel, be pleased with these oblations.
In him, through our sacred prayer (*brahman*), may we worship for the sake of favor, well-being, progeny, sight, cattle, and kindled *jātavedas*.
In which limb does his ascetic heat (*tapas*) reside? In which limb is his cosmic order (*ṛta*) established?
Where does his vow stand? Where does his faith abide? In which limb is his truth established? //1//
From which limb does his fire blaze? From which limb does Mātariśvan blow? From which limb does the moon measure itself out, measuring the limb of the great Skambha? //2//
In which limb does his earth abide? In which limb does the intermediate space abide? In which limb does the sky rest? In which limb does that which is beyond the sky abide? (10.7.3)
Seeking what does Agni blaze upward? Seeking what does Mātariśvan blow? Tell me of that Skambha toward whom the returning winds rush; who indeed is he? //4//
Where do the half-months go? Where do the months go, in harmony with the year? Tell me of that Skambha where the seasons and the seasonal periods go; who indeed is he? //5//
Where do the two young women of different forms, Day and Night, hasten together as they seek him?
Tell me of that pillar where the waters, seeking him, come together; what indeed is it?
Tell me of that Skambha, by supporting which Prajāpati held all the worlds; indeed, who is he? //7//
Whatever was highest, lowest, and that which was middle—the omniform Prajāpati created.
To what extent did Skambha enter therein? And how much was that which he did not enter? //8//

To what extent has Skambha entered into what has come to be? To what extent does he lie within what is yet to be? When he made one limb into a thousand parts, to what extent did Skambha enter therein? //9//
Tell me of that pillar (*skambha*) where people know the worlds, the treasuries, and the waters as Brahman; where the non-existent and the existent meet—what indeed is it?
(10) Where ascetic heat (*tapas*), having exerted itself, maintains the supreme vow (*vrata*). (11)
Where truth and faith, the waters, and the Brahman are concentrated—that Skambha, tell me, who indeed is he? (11)
Tell me of that Skambha upon whom the earth, the intermediate space, and the sky are set; where fire, the moon, the sun, and the wind stand fixed—tell me, who indeed is he? 12.
Tell me of that Skambha, upon whose limb all the thirty-three gods are fully established; who indeed is he? 13.
Where the first-born seers, the *ṛc*, the *sāman*, and the great *yajus* [are found], and where the Single Seer is established—tell me of that Skambha; who indeed is he? //14//
Wherein both immortality and death are contained within the Person;
wherein the ocean and the channels are contained within the Person—tell me of that Skambha; who indeed is he? 15.
In whom the four primary channels stand directed toward the quarters, wherein the sacrifice has exerted its power—tell me of that Skambha; who indeed is he? 16.
Those who know the Brahman in man, they know Parameṣṭhin;
he who knows Parameṣṭhin and he who knows Prajāpati—those who know the eldest Brāhmaṇa, they have fully known Skambha. 17.
He whose head is Vaiśvānara, whose eyes were the Aṅgirases, whose limbs were the Yātus—tell me of that Skambha; who indeed is he? 18.
Tell me of him of whom they say that *brahman* is his mouth and his tongue is the stalk of honey; of whom they say that *virāj* is his udder and *skambha* is his [support]. Who indeed is he? 19.

From whom they carved out the *ṛc* verses, from whom they drew forth the *yajus* formulas, whose hairs are the *sāman* chants, and whose mouth is the *Atharvāṅgirasaḥ*—tell me of that Skambha; who indeed is he?
People know him as the supreme, like something beyond, though he stands supported by the non-existent as his branch.
And even those who are inferior think thus, they who worship your branch. //21//
Wherein the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus are gathered together; wherein both the past and the future, and all the worlds, are established—tell me of that Skambha: who indeed is he? 22.
Whose treasure the thirty-three gods always guard— who today knows that treasure which you, O gods, protect? 23.
Where the gods who know Brahman worship Brahman as the eldest—whosoever should know them directly, he would be a knower of Brahman, a true Brahmā. //24//
Those gods who were born from non-existence are named the Bṛhantas;
people say that one part of Skambha exists beyond them.
Where Skambha, bringing forth the ancient,
turned it about— that one limb of Skambha they have understood as the ancient.
He whose limbs the thirty-three gods divided among themselves—those very thirty-three gods, some who know Brahman indeed know. 27.
People know the Golden Embryo as supreme and unsurpassed; in the beginning, Skambha poured that gold into the world between [the two]. 28.
Upon the Skambha are the worlds; upon the Skambha is ascetic heat; upon the Skambha is the Truth established.
O Skambha, I know you directly: in you, Indra, everything is contained. 29.
In Indra are the worlds, in Indra is heat; in Indra is the Truth established.
I know you, O Indra, face to face: everything is established upon the Support.
He calls aloud name by name, even before the sun and before the dawn.
That which the Unborn first came into being—that indeed he attained as his own sovereignty; than which no other being is higher. //31//
To him whose body is the earth, whose belly is the mid-air, and who made heaven his head—to that supreme Brahman, homage! 32.
To him whose eye is the sun and whose moon is ever-renewed, who made fire his mouth—to that supreme Brahman, obeisance! 33.
Homage to that eldest Brahman, whose out-breath and in-breath are the wind, whose eyes became the Aṅgirasas, and who made the quarters his guides. //34//

The Support has held up both these, heaven and earth; the Support has held up the wide intermediate space. The Support has held up the six wide directions; the Support has entered this entire world. //35//
Homage to that eldest Brahman, who was born from the toil of ascetic heat, who has pervaded all worlds, and who made Soma his own alone. //36//
How is it that the wind does not stop? How is it that the mind finds no rest?
Why is it that the waters, seeking truth, never cease their flow?
A great Yakṣa stands in the midst of the world, having ascended into the heat upon the surface of the waters.
Upon him rest all those who are gods, like branches spreading around the trunk of a tree. //38//
To whom the gods always offer tribute with their hands, their feet, their speech, their hearing, and their sight—within the measured space, tell me of that immeasurable Skambha; who indeed is he? 39.
His darkness is struck away; he is turned back from evil. Within him are all the lights that are in Prajāpati. 40.
He who knows the golden reed standing in the water—he indeed is the secret Prajāpati. //41//
Two young women of different forms weave the warp, treading upon the six-stranded thread.
One draws out the threads, the other holds them; they do not cease their work, nor do they reach the end.
Of those two, as if they were dancing, I do not discern which is further away.
A man weaves this; men sing it aloud; a man has brought this up to the firmament.
(10.7.44a) These rays have propped up the sky; they have made the *sāman* chants their weaving threads for the wind.
{25} (10.8.1a) To him who presides over all that has been and all that is to be, (10.8.1c) and who alone is the master of his own domain—to that eldest Brahman, homage!
By the Skambha these two, heaven and earth, are propped up and stand firm;
this entire world, whatever possesses breath and whatever blinks, is the Skambha.
Three generations have passed beyond; others have settled around the hymn.
The lofty measurer of the mid-region has stood firm; he has entered the tawny, golden-hued mares.
Twelve are the spokes, the wheel is one, and there are three hubs—who indeed has understood that?
Therein are three hundred and sixty stakes, immovable pins.
O Savitṛ, discern this: there are six twins, and one who is born alone. They seek the state of being a mother for him who among them is the one born alone. //5//
Manifest yet hidden in the cave, wearing out its name, is the great station;
therein all this is set—whatever moves and breathes is established.
The single-wheeled [chariot] rolls with its single rim; it has a thousand syllables, moving forward and backward.
With one half he generated the entire world; where was that other half of his? //7//
The five-yoked team carries them at the head; the harnessed side-horses follow along.
His coming was seen, but his going away is not seen—neither the further, nor the nearer, nor the closer, nor the more distant. //8//
A ladle with its opening horizontal and its bottom turned upward—in it glory of every form is deposited.
There sit together the seven seers who were the guardians of this great one. //9//

(10) That which is yoked in front, and that which is yoked behind, that which is yoked on all sides, and that which is yoked everywhere; that by which the sacrifice is extended toward the east—of you, I ask: which one among the *ṛc*s is that?
(11) That which moves, that which flies, and that which stands still; that which breathes and that which does not breathe, and whatever exists that blinks its eyes.
That supports the earth in all its forms; having come together, it becomes one alone. //11//
Endless and spread out in many places, endless yet with an end, reaching to the limits—Nākapāla moves about, discerning that which has been and that which is to be of this [world]. 12.
Prajāpati moves within the womb, unseen; he is born manifoldly.
With one half he has procreated the entire world; what is that sign which is his other half? //13//
All see with their eyes him who carries the water upward as if with a jar; yet not all know him with their mind. //14//
One dwells far from the full; one is left far behind by the deficient.
A great Yakṣa is in the midst of the world; to him the upholders of the realm bring tribute. //15//
From where the sun rises and where it goes to set—that indeed I consider the eldest; nothing whatsoever surpasses that. //16//
Those who, whether from the present, the middle, or the past, speak around the one who knows the Veda—they all speak around Āditya alone, [around] Agni as the second, and the threefold Haṃsa. 17.17
The two wings of this golden swan, flying to heaven, extend over a thousand days’ journey.
Having placed all the gods upon his breast, he goes along beholding all the worlds. 18.
By truth he burns upward; by the sacred word (*brahman*) he looks downward;
by the vital breath (*prāṇa*) he breathes across—that in which the highest is established. //19//
Whoever indeed should know your two kindling-sticks (*araṇī*) from which wealth is churned forth—he, being wise, would consider himself the eldest; he would know the great Brahman.
In the beginning, the footless came into being; he brought forth the light in the beginning.
Having become four-footed, he became an object of enjoyment and took all food for himself. //21//
He becomes one who enjoys, and he bestows much food—
whosoever shall worship the eternal God who possesses the highest realm.
They call him eternal, yet today he may be renewed;
day and night are born from one another’s forms. 23.
A hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million—countless wealth is established in this [person].
While he looks on, they destroy that wealth of his; therefore, this god shines thus. //24//
One [atom] is subtler than a child, and yet another is not seen at all;
therefore, that deity who embraces it is dear to me.
This beautiful, ageless, immortal woman lies in the house of a mortal;
he for whom she was made lies there, and he who made her has grown old.
You are a woman, you are a man; you are a boy or even a girl.
You, when aged, totter along with a staff; you, once born, become one whose face is turned in every direction. //27//
Whether it be their father or their son, whether it be the eldest among them or the youngest—there is but one God who has entered into the mind; he was born first, and he is within the womb.
From the full, the full is drawn up; the full is poured by the full. May we today know that from which it is poured out. (29)
This ancient one was born from the very beginning; this primordial goddess has encompassed everything.
The great goddess Uṣas, shining forth, looks out with each and every twinkling eye.
{28} She whose name is indeed Avīr, the goddess, sits surrounded by Ṛta.
By her beauty, these trees have become green and wear green garlands.
Being near, it does not abandon; being near, it does not see.
Behold the poetic power of the god: he neither dies nor grows old. //32//
Impelled from the unknown, these voices speak according to their respective natures;
where they go while speaking, that they call the Great Brahman. 33.
Where gods and humans are joined together like spokes in a nave—
there I ask you about the flower of the waters, where it is established by *māyā*.
Those by whom the wind, impelled, blows forth; those who give the five directions together;
those gods who disregarded the oblation—who were they that led the waters? 35.
One of these clothes this earth; one has encompassed the intermediate space.
He who is the distributor gives them heaven; others guard all the quarters.
He who knows the thread stretched out, upon which these creatures are woven; he who knows the thread of the thread—he would know the Great Brahman. //37//
I know the thread stretched out, in which these creatures are woven; I know the thread of the thread, and also that which is the great Brāhmaṇa. 38.38
When Agni, all-consuming, went forth burning between heaven and earth,
where the women with their single husbands stood beyond— where indeed was Mātariśvan at that time?
Mātariśvan entered the waters; the gods had entered, and the waters were there.
Lofty indeed he stands, the measurer of the mid-air; as he purifies himself, he has entered the bay steeds.
As if beyond the *gāyatrī*, he has stepped forth upon the immortal;
those who through the *sāman* have understood the *sāman*—where was that Unborn One seen?
The abode and gatherer of riches, like the god Savitṛ whose laws are true,
he stands in the contest for wealth like Indra.
The lotus with nine gates is enveloped by the three qualities;
that which is the conscious spirit within it, the knowers of Brahman truly know as Brahman.
(10.8.44a) Free from desire, wise, immortal, self-existent, satisfied by the essence, he is not deficient in any respect;
(10.8.44c) knowing him alone, the wise one does not fear death—he who is the self, undecaying and ever-youthful.
{29} (10.9.1a) Bind the mouths of those who seek to harm us, and hurl the thunderbolt at our rivals!
The first hundred-porridge offering, given by Indra, is the slayer of rivals and the path for the sacrificer. //1//
Let the altar be your hide, and let the sacrificial grass be those hairs that are yours; this cord has seized you by the neck, and let this pressing-stone dance upon you.
(10.9.3) Let those fools be your sprinkling waters; let the tongue wipe you clean, O inviolable one.
Having become pure and worthy of sacrifice, go forth to heaven, O Śataudana! 3.
He who cooks the hundred-porridge is fulfilled by the fulfillment of his desires;
for all his officiating priests, being gratified, go each to their respective places. 4.
He ascends to heaven, where that triple heaven of the sky is,
who gives the hundred-porridge offering, having made it with a cake as its center.
He attains all those worlds, both celestial and terrestrial,
who gives the hundred-porridge oblation after making it radiant with gold.
O Goddess Śataudanā, those who are your pacifiers and those people who are your cooks—they shall all protect you; do not fear them. (AVŚ 10.9.7)
